Listen, I’m not saying Cliff is a bad guy, but my pharmacist is about to go out of business because of him. Here is a draft of that story, punch-up comedian style. Feel free to post this on your socials—it’s got that "relatable academic trauma" vibe that usually does numbers. The Cure for Insomnia (Or: Why My Pharmacist Hates Cliff) I’ve been on prescription-strength melatonin for years, right? My blood is basically 40% cherry-flavored sleep aid. I thought I was a medical mystery—a man whose brain simply refused to log off. Then I met Cliff. Cliff doesn’t give lectures; he performs "auditory anesthesia." His voice isn’t a human voice—it’s the sound of a dial-up modem trying to connect in a rainstorm. It’s the sonic equivalent of watching beige paint dry in slow motion. Last week, I walked into Cliff’s room, he said, "Good morning, class, let's look at the sub-sections of paragraph B," and I was out. I didn’t just nap; I entered a coma so deep I saw my ancestors. My Fitbit actually sent a notification to my emergency contacts because it thought I had passed away. I’ve officially cancelled my prescription. Why pay a $20 co-pay for pills when I can just sit in the back row of Cliff's class for free? He is a biological miracle. If we could bottle his energy, we could solve the world’s stress levels in a weekend, mostly because everyone would be unconscious. The only problem? Anwar. See, I actually want to pass Course 330. Anwar is the problem because he’s actually... engaging? He’s funny, he’s got energy, he makes 330 feel like a Netflix special. I’m sitting there in Anwar’s class, wide awake, learning things, and laughing. It’s disgusting. I’m actually retaining information. So now I have a system: I go to Anwar to pass the degree. I go to Cliff to achieve the deepest REM cycle known to man. If you see me sprinting from Anwar’s room to Cliff’s, don’t worry. I’m just heading to my bedroom.

He's just plain terrible. While I'm happy I took the class and I learned a great deal, none of this is thanks to Pete. He's a flat-out terrible lecturer, and doesn't seem to have much going on between the ears. The projects are helpful as an introduction to kernel development, but Pete's name is nowhere to be found on the projects, nor on GeekOS (the class's operating system). 80% of what I learned in this class was from the textbook and the projects, both of which can be found for free online. The exams are awful. They test you on almost entirely minutia rather than your true understanding of the concepts. It makes no difference in real life if you can recall the exact semantics of a file system, as documentation is more accurate than memory 100% of the time. Almost all of the points I lost in the class were from exams, and I didn't even care toward the end of the class. I ended about half a point under an A-. One of the terms we were asked to define on the exam was not on any course slides, nor in the textbook. On one occasion, Pete himself had a solution incorrect in his answer key. He also, as another reviewer has mentioned, asked ChatGPT to generate him lecture material without so much as proofreading it. This class made me realize that I'm just about done with academics, and I'm now planning to graduate early. This class is an absolute joke, and the incompetency on display here has opened my eyes to how out-of-touch college departments are. Students are paying thousands of dollars in tuition a year, and yet we receive half-assed lectures from a man with maybe one brain cell in his head. You can learn all of this online if you have the motivation. Get your piece of paper, get out, and write some free and open source software. Do some good for the world, lest you become a living zombie inhabiting the dying wasteland of a university like Peter Keleher.

I would only recommend this class if you have a light semester or elite ball time management skills. - Marsh uses a flipped classroom, where he demos random stuff during class and makes you watch videos on your own. The videos are far from enough to do the projects, but you can't just skip them and self study, because there's a Canvas quiz for each one. - For the first 2 projects, there's a "follow up" where you live code in front of a TA. The coding tasks themselves aren't too bad, but the logistics are awful. There was a period where they ran out of appointments, and various announcements from Marsh and different TAs contradicted each other. It felt like they hardly communicated with each other and didn't coordinate plans at all. - He uses "standards-based grading," where grades are based on checklists of assignment statuses. For example, you need x projects at 100%, x writeups at excellent, x writeups at sufficient, etc. This made things ambiguous when you didn't match checklists perfectly and were between letter grades. FWIW, the class content is quite interesting imo and Marsh seems like a nice guy. He just has some really *creative* ideas on how to run a class.

TLDR: Prof's okay, course is really bad. You will learn nothing, buts its an ez A. Worst course I've taken IN MY LIFE, not just in college. My 8th grade art lessons were better. Pros: 2 reasons to take it: ez A, or you're in the ML track. PS: Im not saying Regli is a bad professor, I never went to the lectures (watched recordings though). He is very kind, flexible, and willing to accommodate students; he genuinely cares about you as a person and wants you to succeed. He is also basically omnipresent on emails, and you pretty much never have to wait more than a day. I got multiple responses from him within 10 minutes to an hour. If you have to reschedule a quiz, he basically leaves it up to your TA. His TAs are chill, so this is completely fine. He is very willing to let you reschedule exams in a timely manner, even if you don't provide documentation. I was having a breakdown with 4 exams in a single week, and he didn't miss a beat, replying in like 10 minutes, accepting my requests without any pushback. He has more-or-less weekly quizzes and worksheets. Worksheets are graded on effort, so just do them and try each question, and he'll give you a 100. If you can't make it to class, just email him, and he'll send you the worksheet and have you email it to your TA. I've never gotten anything less than 100 in his class, but from what I've heard, he is very generous with partial credit if you make a small algebra mistake but demonstrate that you understand the concept he taught you. He also often doesn't require you to simplify answers, which means there's less chance of making small algebraic mistakes. His exams are also extremely fair because they have way fewer questions than most other professors (usually 5-6), so it's not nearly as much of a race against the clock. He's also not trying to trick you; he gives you questions that are very similar to those on practice exams. No WebAssign or MATLAB homeworks, just suggested problems for each quiz. You don't have to do these, but you should, so you can practice for quizzes. I already learned Calculus 1 through 3 in high school, but I just didn't take the AP exams, so lectures are kind of irrelevant to me. However, from what I've heard from people who didn't, his lectures are extremely helpful. Not derivation-heavy, pretty much just examples of problems you'll have to solve. If we don't get to something, he'll adjust the quizzes accordingly, so as to ensure you don't have to study on your own.

Before I get into my review, I should note that the C+ is pretty much entirely on me. I should have taken the course more seriously, especially for the first midterm, and I got burned for not doing so. At least I passed. With that said, this class did not work for me whatsoever. It's not because the class is hard, though it absolutely is, and I'd argue it should be. I just don't think it's for the right reasons. For instance, the lecture/exam half of the course is almost entirely disjoint from the GeekOS project half of the course, and it really feels like a 5/6 credit course sometimes. Being good at the lecture content will not help you whatsoever with GeekOS, and vice versa. This seems to be a 412-wide issue. Regarding the lecture content, I don't think Pete is a very good lecturer. It's sort of what the other reviewers this semester so far have pointed out. I wouldn't quite agree with the tin can rattling mentality, but he certainly doesn't practice his presentations, and he brings absolutely no energy to the class. Another reviewer pointed out the ChatGPT image, which he said he would fix and never did, but there was another instance where he took a TRIO slide set from the internet, didn't review it at all beforehand, and tried going through it in a rather miserable showing. There's very little transformation of his slide content in his lectures, as all he does is take his laser pointer and point to things he wants to emphasize on one of the projectors in the room. The slides themselves are rather poor summaries of OSTEP, which he follows very closely. That's just lectures themselves. The assignments he gives aren't much better in my opinion. He assigns weekly Gradescope reading homeworks which are worth 1% of the grade each. I honestly almost wish he would give more traditional homeworks instead. Some of the questions are horribly ambiguous, there's no room to state any assumptions, there are some questions where it feels like even with both the slides and OSTEP you can't really answer well, they ultimately lack engagement, and they are nowhere near comprehensive enough to actually prepare for the exams imo. Regarding exams, exam 1 was insane with the short answer questions of random topics from the slides being worth so much of the grade, while exams 2 and 3, especially 3, were relatively more chill. These certainly weren't my strongsuit, as I'm horrible with memorizing topics which I haven't worked directly with in some meaningful way, and I'm rather terrible at studying. I didn't like them, but they were fine I guess. One question I would like to address is the barber shop semaphore problem in exam 2. Not only were the semantics poorly defined, as the professor admitted, but in my experience, semaphore programming isn't just something just I get right away. I haven't worked with them before, as I haven't had any need to. They really weren't gone over well in class, nor were the gradescope assignments enough to really nail it in. He didn't give any other practice problem on them besides the baboon problem from a reading homework. I realize this is just one specific example, but it's emblematic of my problem with this part of the class as a whole. I also realize this could just be me, and my review should be taken with at least a grain of salt due to my meager performance compared to the rest of the class. I didn't mention this before, but each exam was 15%, and there was no final exam. Regarding GeekOS, the TA's, especially Leo, really carried here. They were really helpful in getting some of the projects working, and I really wouldn't have passed the class without them. Though, I'd maybe argue they were a bit too necessary to get through the projects. It's very clear the project specs haven't been updated in years, and the project slides, especially for the later projects such as 4b and all of 5, don't seem at all sufficient in getting you through the projects. Of course, the projects should be challenging, but in my experience, there was a lot of frustration due to how much information the slides and specs omit. For example, in project 5, file systems, GFS3 is a completely proprietary file system, yet we're not really given a good specification of it. For example, we were only given one example GFS3 image whose structure is completely undocumented. In project 4b, demand paging (the hardest project imo, though I hated 5 more just by nature), the way in which we were basically required to do things isn't very easy to deduce from source code, and the slides honestly made it more confusing what we had to do. Don't get me wrong, these projects are pretty cool at the end of the day, and honestly it was very useful being forced to navigate and implement significant components into a Linux-like kernel. I just think the projects would be better if the provided resources were more helpful. Finally, there's grading. The class is graded on a curve. This semester, seemingly a lot of insanely smart people took the class, which seemingly skewed the grade distribution like crazy. There was a review last semester of someone getting an 88 with Dr. Agrawala and ending with an A+. I know someone who got like an 89 this semester and ended with an A-. Take that for what you will. Overall, I can't say I don't recommend taking this class at all, but I have some issues with it. Pete is teaching this class next spring, so it seems for a little bit, Dr. Agrawala and Pete are alternating teaching this class.

The projects aren't easy but they're all easier than some of the ones you do in 330, in my opinion, and that's a required course. In summary - If you just want to coast, you can do that easily. And if you want to really learn the material, this class gives you the freedom and time to do so because you don't have to stress about exams.

I want to start off by saying that Justin took a lot of feedback from this semester, and I don't think he's going to be doing 7 midterms again lol (i could be wrong). The class structure was 7 midterm exams, with your lowest score to be dropped, which he changed to two at the end of the semester, 6 projects, lowest dropped, and then a final take home which was very easy cause its open note and you have time to just check your notes for the answer (he says you wont but if you I did this and still had like 45 minutes of time to spare). Overall the lectures were really well taught, and you can tell he puts effort into thinking how to make it understandable for students. The exams were annoying since they were every two weeks, with means of ~83. Again at the end of the semester he was very gracious in taking feedback, and ended up dropping a 2nd exam. The whole semester I thought I was going to end up with an A-, but he ended up dropping the grade boundary all the way to 91, combined with the dropping of exams if you do all the projects its not too difficult to get an A. I probably would have given him a 3 star, but him taking feedback sincerely was nice so I think he deserves a 4. But still, I think he kind of went overkill with the 7 exams. This is hands down the worst course I've taken all my life, not just in college. This is more of a review for the course than the professor, Regli is chill (judging from the one time I met him). It IS a very easy class: cheat sheet, ez homeworks, broad material. Why the poor rating? The course structure, specifically the syllabus. This is a very broad class, concepts and terms are mentioned, basic parts of algorithms are taught, but you will not end up taking anything from the course. The only way for you to truly understand whats going on is if you read the book, the additional material along with the slides and visit office hours, etc. Exams seem like a test of can-you-create-the-best-cheatsheet. To me, it felt like a terminology class, does X mean this, etc. Exams being MCQs is another big factor of why this course is stupid. I should also add that this course is about GOFAI (good old fashioned AI) which means its almost entirely irrelevant to anything ML (there's minor relevance to robotics and RL, but thats it) Reasons to take this class: you want to do the ML track (which was my reason), you want an ez A Reasons not to take to class: if you care about your time/course choice or If you want to learn smth. I personally feel like unless you are solidifying your GPA, choice of 4XXs matters. I would say if do not fall in the category above, DO NOT take this class. You will genuinely learn nothing. My 8th grade art class where I never did anything but painted one canvas was more of a learning experience for me. PS: Again, Regli's chill and its the syllabus that is crap. I should add that I never went to class and only showed up for exams, so make of this review what you will (although idt attending class will help much, the material is too broad, concepts are never explained properly, its all way too rushed)

As a graduating senior, this is one of the classes that I have found most valuable to my education. The course content is high level and relevant. Class time is not wasted learning or doing things that do not matter. Lecture is where we learn, discussion is where we code together. This gives you the tools you need to complete the only assignments for the course- articles that you write and post on a topic of your choosing. What I like about this is that we will leave the class with tangible evidence of our learning that we can show off on our resume or to recruiters in the future. I can't say enough good things about this professor or this course. This is how all classes should be structured in my opinion. I highly highly recommend taking this course with Professor Buntain.

I think Teli is alright, but still a good choice for 250. He doesn't explain things very clearly, but he makes up for this by going through a lot of examples in depth during lecture. You're left with a strong understanding on how to answer questions correctly, but with hazy knowledge on why you format the steps in the way you're supposed to, especially since some of the TAs will format their proofs or answer problems a bit differently than Teli did. It's not a problem for most of the semester--the midterms are incredibly easy, easier than the practice exams. The content in the course only really gets difficult between the second midterm and the final, and since the final isn't cumulative, there's no easy content from the beginning to pad it; but still very doable if you study well. The quizzes are sometimes easy, sometimes difficult--definitely study for those, especially as you get further into the semester. Homeworks are challenging, so don't slack off on those either. Overall, the negatives of his lecturing style don't really show themselves until you reach the end of the course, and even then just skimming the recommended textbook helps solidify the things he doesn't go over as much. I complain about his lecturing style a lot, but honestly he is a solid choice for 250 and I would recommend; put in the work, and it's not difficult to get an A.

My review won't be as critical as the other one for this semester, but I share a lot of the sentiments about Pete and the class. Pete himself admitted that his info about this topic in general is out of date one class, and his generally subpar lecturing style (very monotone) leads to a lot of confusion and difficulty understanding content. We follow an online (free) textbook which goes into more detail, but a lot of the content on the exams is either difficult to find in the textbook or just something he put on a couple slides. The exams themselves aren't difficult given you scour the slides and your notes. All the problems on the exam are either short form questions about certain topics or definitions, or questions you've seen before on homeworks. The projects are on the more difficult side compared to other 4XX classes, and set up similar to 417 where they're tangentially related to what we're currently learning about in class, but most of the work is figuring out how to implement the features within the existing GeekOS system. I personally really enjoyed these projects, they were interesting and fun to work with. The difference though between this class and 417 though, is that the project specs are rather useless. They don't really help much with understanding what you're doing at all to be honest, and its hard to get a grasp of the scope of each project purely from the spec sheets. It's not impossible, but there's a noticeable difference that leads to a worse experience. However, the issues with projects is all offset by the TA Leo. For every project, he provided a video and slides that allowed us to work our way through each project step by step. He gave us good tips and ideas during OH, and basically led the project part of the course.

Solely judging on how "easy" the class is, I would give it a 4 stars. The buffer overflows project was the only extremely difficult one, the other's just took some time, but nothing crazy. In terms of how much I learned, I would give this class a 2 stars. I will say, I actually went to lecture 75% of the time so I probably got more out of the class than people who never went so that's on them. Marsh's teaching style was ... alright. I think a flipped classroom CAN work, but I don't think it was the best in this case, especially given the fact that there was SOOOO much content. (I also just find it really hard to focus when watching videos). I don't agree with the reviews, below, it really was not that bad. Some of the quizzes were a little confusing, but you had unlimited attempts at them. His grading scale was also incredibly fair (he used a EMRN scale for writing instead of grading with numbers), and as long as you started the work before it was due, it was pretty manageable. I believe he's planning on removing the late deadlines, but this is probably a good thing. I know a lot of people let work pile up at the end of the semester and it hurt their grade. The group project SUCKED, but mostly because I had a terrible group who waited until a week before it was due to even look at the project. The instructions were a little confusing but if you spoke with a TA or Marsh early it made a bit more sense. It wasn't necessarily hard, just a bit confusing on what we were supposed to protect against. There were also no exams which was a huge bonus in my opinion. I started the semester seriously freaked out about this class, but after I figured out the buffer overflows project, which admittedly took me forever, I found the rest to be pretty easy. Everyone says this but just start the projects early and speak to TAs or Marsh when you get stuck, it really helps.

I honestly think Professor Rudinger deserves a higher rating. Starting with the good: The lectures were interesting and informative, offering clear explanations of complex topics. Professor Rudinger was very helpful during office hours and genuinely cared about students’ understanding. HWs and exams are not difficult, and I felt that they reflected the course content well. Also, the new grading structure (gone is the 45% final, its weight split between an additional midterm and final) was a positive change, making the overall grade distribution more balanced. Formula sheets were allowed for every exam, which was helpful. However, there are still quite a few areas for improvement: Students’ questions on Piazza often went unanswered for days. I really liked this course. Fardina is super nice and genuinely cares about her students. I interacted with her a lot during class and also asked many questions after class and she was always patient and took the time to help me understand what I was trying to do. The homework was straightforward and helpful. The midterms were a bit long, but the final exam was very doable and fair. Overall, it was a great experience for me and I learned a lot.

Not good at teaching and very good at making simple things hard and hard things impossible. Take Anwar if you can. If you must take him, either go to Anwar's lectures & study/review based on his notes or go to Cliff's lectures and risk annoying the entire class by asking questions every 10 minutes because he can't teach without confusing people like so.

You probably know the drill about Nelson by now. He's a funny dude who is a great lecturer.. when he stays on topic and isn't making crude or inappropriate jokes. I was surprised by how much I learned from this class. I feel more knowledgeable about JavaScript and different web frameworks as a whole. You don't need to go to lectures. Exams are copy paste from the semester before. I won't detract stars from Nelson for this, but his grading TAs are a pain to deal with.
very nice guy good at explaining stuff. only bad thing is the pacing of the content

He's not a bad teacher for CMSC411. You don't study a lot of material in this class, but you're expected to know the concepts you are taught like the back of your hand. We had 3 exams (including the final) worth about 16% of your grade each. I thought all were very fair, which surprised me. The only tricky part was the T/F which tested you on a bunch of technicalities. There were 2 projects, both written in C. However, I thought the projects had no business being in C, as everything you simulate and implement could have been done in Python or any other high-level language to avoid the hassle that comes with low-level programming. The 5 homeworks were fine. They took me on average 3 hours each and I averaged an 88 on them. Overall, I wouldn't urge you to not take his class, but I wouldn't suggest scrambling to get a seat in it. -1 stars for the projects being a little unorganized, and -1 for sort of dry course content. Nothing bad to say about Dr. Yoon himself.

This guy has a legit tin can rattling around upstairs instead of a brain. Every lecture, he acts as if he sees his slides for the first time. He's always confused by his own slides, and half of them have wrong information. One class period, he had a time diagram that made no sense, which he then revealed was because he asked ChatGPT to generate it. His sloth-like energy didn't even bother to check the image after "sticking it into ChatGPT". The projects are really hard but they are honestly very fun. The content of the course is very interesting, but the professor doesn't know what he's talking about. Shout out to the TA Leo, however. That guy is beyond awesome and super helpful in office hours.

good! i liked him pros: great lecturer projects were very interesting class is very applicable to software, literally working through system design and potential vulnerabilities you can come across cons: class is messy, some disconnect between project release dates and overall communication some of the projects are p hard, but that's to be expected ull learn a lot

Just a note about the really bad warnings: we were only told that he was switching his class format about two weeks before the semester started so I would guess that some people who were really unhappy may not have had enough time to find a new class or realized what 7 exams would entail for them (especially poor test takers). Yes, 7 exams could be stressful (this is the reason I deducted a star, but really I'd give a 4.5 if possible). However, the exams were really fair except for the first one. They were a lot like the recommended problems, some of them were even directly from these problems. For anyone who doesn't struggle with serious test anxiety, you'll probably be fine. Do the recommended problems and try to stay on top of content so you don't have to cram for each exam. Justin himself is a great teacher. His lectures were pretty engaging and he explained things really well. The only real complaint I have about the exams is that sometimes the proofs were just a little too difficult for someone who isn't used to proofs. The first exam was kind of heinous, but I think Justin just didn't account for the fact that it had been awhile since we had seen 351 material and we all had professors who taught the content differently. And Justin is INCREDIBLY nice, like way nicer than a professor really has to be. He wasn't out to get us with the 7 exam thing, he was just trying to make the course fair to those of us who refuse to cheat on every single assignment handed to us. He dropped an extra exam after seeing how much stress some of the students were experiencing due to the change in class structure. He extended project deadlines MULTIPLE times. Again, as long as you're not someone who has serious test anxiety you will do fine.

Nice guy, and a rockstar in the field. However, a lot of his lectures made no damn sense when I didn't have prior background or experience with the material. He would essentially just talk through mathematical notation or code without laying out any conceptual roadmap for the algorithm or technique we were doing, which results in me thinking that none of this is really going to stick in my brain after class. Office hours where I could talk with him one-on-one with more dialogue-y teaching was only slightly more improved. For morning lectures he himself would not so uncommonly get confused on what the hell was going on in his slides and have to spend some time to figure out what he even wanted to say. On final exam review, he got a non-insignificant portion of his own questions wrong.

Tough course. Slides were not very helpful. Homeworks were pretty interesting but I didn't really feel like they were very helpful when it came to exams. What made the biggest difference to me was doing all of the reading for each topic. The week before the final, I watched every single lecture video and did every single reading and got a 90. I don't know if it was just me, but I found it really hard to pay attention during in person lecture.

It's a very chill class with him and he teaches fairly well. However, a third of the content that was on quizes or exams were based on straight memorization like do you remember the library that allows you to do this. Also, the wording on the last quiz, homework, and exam was a bit confusing and very stubborn in terms of accepting a different interpretation of his vague questions. Other than those 2 complaints it's a chill class.

If you're going to take CMSC430, take it with DVH! He is super knowledgeable and it's clear his sole goal of the class it to make sure everybody learns something. He welcomes questions and engagement during class, and really turns lecture into what the class makes it. The notes are extensive and helpful, and assignments are weekly, but short. There are 2 exams, which are 24-hour take-home projects. They don't actually take 24 hours, and you can probably get full points if you just pay attention in lecture and do the assignments. The final was a final project that was also pretty manageable. Course staff was responsive to questions on Piazza as well. Highly recommend DVH. He's understanding, kind, and good at explaining things. In my opinion, the way DVH lectured made this class even easier than the compilers unit in CMSC330.

This class might be the most useless class I have taken at UMD. The class isn't that bad, and the projects were fine. He added a final exam worth 25% (which wasn't too difficult). My only complaint is honestly with myself, as I feel like I wasted my time on this class. He gave 1% EC because 90% of the students completed the course eval, which was a nice thing. He took attendance at least once a week on average on GradeScope (worth 5% of your overall grade), so be aware. He does record lectures, so that's a plus. Just look at his website for 433 online and see if you could benefit from learning the material. In my opinion, it is the most useless class (but well, that just might be me, so...). Otherthan that, if you put the effort, it should be decently easy to get an A. Not like a free A class, but very fair to do well.

Awesome lecturer, very fair exams, very nice guy. I sent him an email about something and then went to office hours two weeks later and as soon as I walked in he somehow knew my name and remembered I had emailed(we had never spoken before). Broke down complex topics very simply. We did have 5 quizzes instead of homeworks(shout out to Spring 2025 for using AI on the HW), but one dropped and he gave pretty big hints as to exactly what would be on there. He also offered to let us submit HWs for feedback if we got a different solution than the answer key which I didn't end up using but probably should have. In my opinion it made studying for the final easier because I had already been studying manageable chunks every three weeks. Highly recommend this course - it was super interesting, albeit challenging but definitely a super valuable part of my experience.

Professor Doboszczak is a great professor. As an engineering major I have taken just a few math courses throughout my degree.... and Stefan is definitely one of the best I've had. He doesn't just go over the most basic example in lecture and give you the hardest problems to solve for homework. He gives a great balance of examples and theoretical explanations and gives challenging but solvable homework problems. He gives great practice exams and plenty of additional resources to learn the material. The only downside is that he doesn't release answer keys to the practice exams. So you should work on them well before the exam so you can get assistance from him or the TA's if you're stuck. The course, though being titled computational methods, has a lot of cool information regarding the IEEE floating point standard, how computers store numbers, and how to figure out how accurate your answer can be on a given machine (single precision vs double precision). The second half of the course I found to be more challenging as it is the more theoretical mathematical concepts you see on the course description (interpolation, quadrature, differentiation, etc). I was weary to take this class after being required to take so many math courses -- but I actually enjoyed every lecture I watched because of Stefans teaching. I would 100% recommend this course to anyone that has the option to take it.

Professor Rudinger seems like a nice person; when you talk to her, she seems genuine and caring. Her slides were super informative and her lectures were fairly interesting, too. However, the lectures didn't actually add much to the content on the slides that was relevant for exams. If you're so interested in NLP that you'd like to acquire some fun-fact trivia knowledge that won't be tested, feel free to attend her lectures. Otherwise, just read the slides she posts after each class. The biggest issue with Rudinger is her responsiveness. The organization of the class is genuinely horrible. We were meant to have 4 projects this semester, and we ended up having only two. The third was made optional/bonus, as it was released during the final week of the semester with 4 days to complete, and the fourth was scrapped entirely. She rarely (if ever) replies to emails, and the Piazza for this class is the slowest I've had for any CS class at the university thus far. The final is worth 45% of your grade, which is frankly absurd. Almost the entire class's content is better taught in CMSC 472 instead; take that class and you'll come out far more knowledgeable about both NLP and general ML than you will by taking 470.

This guy was great haha some people need to get over themselves. Yeah he takes forever to respond to emails and some of the TAs suck. But I just went to his live discussions and we would go over everything I wanted. He was super nice and very helpful. Find the better TAs too for office hours - its pretty obvious after going a few times. It's a decently easy class if you stay on top of things and I feel like I learned a ton. Will definitely be recommending Prof. Patrick to others.

A really easy class, but not an understanding instructor and definitely not passionate about what he teaches. For the final project my group had all parts of the final graded as a 100%, but we did not submit it the way he wanted and he failed our project anyways. Any attempt to discuss our misunderstanding was met with a cold and rude email. Basically told us to stop talking to him and had us email advising instead. Overall really unprofessional and does not care about his students outside of his paycheck.

She teaches INST 414, at least for Spring 2025. By far the worst professor I had at INFO Sci Dept. Attendance are worth 40% of the grade so if you miss weeks of classes your grades will hit the rock bottom in matter of no time. I do not like how the class is structured cause the class is mostly self-learning. Class only meets twice a week, in each of the classes she makes students to complete worksheets on their on or with partners rather than actually giving lectures. I do not understand why the attendance is mandatory when students can get their worksheets done while being in their home. Also, she is a super harsh grader and have no mercy at all. Another thing is that she doesn't respond to any grade inquiries until the end of the semesters, which makes it hard for students to know if they going to pass the class or not before the withdrawal period. I do not recommend anyone to take this professor cause she is just gonna drain your GPA.

This class was pretty bad. The professor is very nice, but the way the material is taught is not easy to understand at all. We were taught one thing in class but the programming assignments and labs were way harder and sometimes made zero sense. I didn't think this class would be bad at all, I had a lot of hope but it's stressed me a lot this semester, by far my most stressful class.

Great professor if you really want to understand the subject. Teaches a lot from the chalkboard, but he does record and post all his lectures, so there's a lot of flexibility there. Quiz questions were straight from the problem bank and exams were difficult, but not more than you'd expect for a math course like this. Only complaint is the TA's weren't always up to date on the methods and if you don't pay close attention, it's very easy to lose Dr. Williams in his lectures. Overall, good professor to take for this Calculus 1 though.

Pros: -Lectures are very thorough, easy to follow, and contain numerous practice problems that very much prepare you for tests. -No homework. Some may find that as a con, but if you attend his lectures and pay attention, you'll get everything you need to know. -Extremely light grader. One quiz I got basically the entire question wrong from the start, and still received an 85, which was one of two quizzes that he dropped at the end of the semester. -Posts practice exams that are very similar, if not identical, to the midterms you'll be taking. -One of the kindest, most sympathetic, helpful educaters ive ever had. Cons: -I couldnt tell you a single one. TAKE THIS CLASS! CALC 2 IS HARD, BUT HE MAKES IT SEEM LIKE A CAKEWALK!

Just go to his office hours and discussion sessions and trust me it will be smooth sailing. Explains concepts in an understanding way and really cares for his student. Probably the best TA in the entire university.

This guy is overhated, I would give him a 3.5/5 but I'm rounding up because I feel his current rating is unfair. The semester did get off to a rocky start but he quickly improved his teaching and I felt the lectures were easy enough to understand. The homeworks are mostly easy with only one hard proof question per homework with lecture examples being able to guide you. The homeworks usually did enough to prepare for the exams. The quizzes were super easy and were free grade boosters. He's also a super nice guy, he was willing to curve every exam if the average was below 83% and gave so much extra credit on homeworks that my average homework grade ended up being 115%. This professor is nice and caring but that is literally it. I don't even know where to start with this. Lectures are useless, everything he goes over he posts on Canvas, but even then lecture is just a huge information dump without actually being able to apply it. Then we get right into discussion where we have a quiz nearly every week on topics that we had not properly gone over in lecture. There is a single project at the end of the semester and that is it. No homework or assignments other than quizzes, midterm, and final. We are given a practice worksheet for each unit and typically quiz problems are chosen from there but most of the time it is curveball questions that do not test us properly. Having midterm and quiz grades be at an average of a 50 is atrocious, and this professor does nothing well with explaining the content. Really bad, would not recommend you take her as your professor. The projects are not hard, however the exams require you to thoroughly learn the material on your own.

wait i love herman his lectures are so listenable to me for some reason and the mandatory attendance was annoying at first but i found it super helpful in the end. never had to cram for exams too hard and all exams are pretty fair as long as you study every slides posted. listening to the lecture also helps a ton for me, i pretty much listened to 80% of his lectures. he's not a bad option. pls let him stay above 3 rating

Genuinely horific class. There's a ton of reviews that elaborate on why he's so terrible but it really does not compare to how awful it is to actually be in this class. Please, PLEASE do not take Yoon if you can help it. Hell, even if you would have to delay taking this class, that might be preferable if you're already struggling mentally. I mean this seriously. Projects are poorly documented and extremely tedious. Classes are unbelievably boring and nigh unfollowable with how poorly Yoon can actually qualify what he is teaching. Quizzes and exams consist of either extremely tedious coding, very niche knowledge, and the memorization that'll have you wondering whether anything you learn in this class will actually stick with you: it won't. On multiple ocassions you will think this class has drained your passion for CS. I can know state with certain that I still like CS, but that Yoon has doon irreperable damage to my view of UMD and any form of education it could teach me in the subjects that actually matter to me. If this isn't enough to convince you, Kaufman apparently has open notes. Avoid Yoon at all cost.

I took this course in spring 2025 and I can truly say that Fawzi was one of the best lecturers I've had at UMD. I learned so much from attending lecture and he explained topics very well. He would make explanations of topics very thorough and relatable so that they stuck. The discussions were not that useful in my opinion but that is very dependent upon your TA. However, the worksheets given in discussion proved to be very useful. I liked the fact that the homework was not graded because I could use the assignments for practice (I would do the problems then use the answer key to see what he was looking for in terms of format). Also if there was a problem that I could not figure out no matter how much I tried, I could always fall back on his answer key to point me in the right direction to start or learn how to do the problem entirely. Some might say that this "defeats the whole purpose of homework" but I would disagree saying that it made the homework less stressful and allowed me to learn something new rather than simply sitting there not knowing what to do. Overall his exams were very fair and were truly indicative of the content covered in class. Although he did not provide practice exams, reviewing the homework, worksheets, and lecture examples multiple times and ensuring that I was comfortable with those types of problems and the theory behind them was enough to do well. If you are on the fence about taking him, I would do it. If you attend his lectures, pay attention, and put in the work outside of class, you will do very well.

Lectures are chaotic and uninformative, but because of how bad the slides he posts are, you have to go to them to learn the material. Exams had low scores, as 1 midterm and the final had a C- median and 1 midterm had a D median for my section. The questions aren't hard because there are gymnastics involved, they are hard because you get very little exam review material and because most topics are only mentioned offhandedly in the slides, but given conceptual questions on the exams. I would highly recommend completing the homework before the midterm that covers the corresponding topics, as the hw is the best (and only) way for you to examine the material better than in lecture. He gives substantial opportunities to improve your grade through extra credit. The bulk of extra credit opportunities are on the hw assignments. Be warned however that even though it is "extra", he considered all of the hw extra credit before he decided on a curve, diminishing the curve to the point that unless you scored an A average on exams, extra credit is almost required to achieve a high grade. He assigned 4 homeworks, all of which were very easy. Normally he just gives extra credit for the vague criteria of a submission being high effort or impressive. Sometimes though he announces specific additions that he will give extra credit for in class. When you consider how easy the homework assignments were, getting the substantial extra credit to give yourself a good shot at an A requires the same amount of effort as the hw for a typical cs class. For each hw, about half of the class got extra credit.

Do not recommend Cliff at all. His lectures are extremely unhelpful and he has a cocky attitude when speaking with students. Also, most of his TAs (besides a couple that were really helpful) never answer student questions on piazza and hold useless discussions. I strongly suggest taking Anwar's section instead. Not only is he a better lecturer, he seems to care more about his students.

The Professor is really nice and funny at times. Attending lectures is not required, and lecture recordings are posted online. For exam preparation, he provides a folder of previous exams for practice, which greatly helps, as it is very similar to the actual exam. The projects are pretty simple and basically require copying and pasting code from the lecture example. There is no final exam, but a group project. Overall, the course is very easy to take and get an A in. If the projects allowed for some flexibility and were more engaging it would have been nice, as I felt like the content really didn't stick with me. Also, since most of the people did not attend lecture, making this class fully online for future semesters could be something to consider.

Worst professor I have ever taken. His handwriting is atrocious and unreadable. His course consists of 5 year old videos and random math theorists. This class is basically all self taught. The exams are extremely difficult and the rubric is very unreasonable. If you don't know how to answer the question leaving it blank is the best answer. Based off the rubric you are either completely right, very close to correct, or wrong and receive no credit. Do not take him.

The lectures were pretty boring and not terribly informative. The class was well structured with only a few homework assignments and projects throughout the semester. Exams were fair and there is practice material provided.

The GOAT professor. I genuinely learned so much about operating systems in this class. The projects are super time-consuming, true, and you have to study a lot for the exams. Still, it's intensely rewarding. The professor is hard but fair, and genuinely knows so much. If you talk to him, you'll realize how nice and knowledgeable he is. If you are willing to put in the time investment, this class is a must-take, in my opinion.

Do not take this class. Flipped classroom whatever. when it comes to that part you should know yourself and your work habits. This is NOT the reason why I think this class was terrible though. "Lectures" teach you absolutely nothing and barely even the concepts of the class, completely ruining the flipped classroom model. The syllabus is closer to a Russian tax code than an actual syllabus. Comparing my experiences to my peers, it's clear to see that which TA grades your projects/follow-ups/challenge problems decides too much of your grade in this course. This class is actually a sham and I genuinely think the CMNS department should review this course's scope and general practices. Marsh as a professor is a very good lecturer and I enjoyed his demos in class but again gave me nothing of value for any graded work in the class.

He talks extremely quietly. He is not technology savvy at all. I firmly believe he has not interacted with Canvas once the entire semester. Everything that wasn't lectures seemed to be run by the TAs. He was present for perhaps half the days of the semester. We covered maybe 20% of the intended curriculum in lecture. Self-teaching is a requirement. Two ridiculous scenarios that occurred: - First assignment of the course and a four part project were about KD-trees. We did not cover KD-trees AT ALL in any lectures. - Some topics that were not in the curriculum showed up on the final.

Kim and Regli were co-teaching this semester, so they had all the same stuff. Kim is better when watching the lecture videos because she draws on the slides themselves, while Regli points to things in person, which isn't shown in the video because we only see the slideshow. She has an accent, but it's nothing too crazy (you can understand her well).

Teli and his Goons (TA's) are a bunch of clowns. These geniuses accidentally made the project 3 grade out of 115 points instead of 100, because there are 15 points of extra credit. Then, when everyone points it out on Piazza, he literally disables the CMSC422 Piazza without fixing it. He just doesn't give a shit, absolute clown boy with his clown mobile and clown goons.
Just read the slides it's all you have to do. And he gives practice quizzes and exams that tell you exactly what to expect. Nice guy

DVH is a somewhat “distant" professor, which is my biggest issue with him. He leaves most of the teaching to the online course notes and only the TAs hold office hours. You can tell he isn’t 100% engaged in the course and, as a consequence, it becomes very difficult to fully engage in the course as a student. There’s nothing super bad about him, but I probably wouldn’t take him again unless I had to.

Not too bad for a 4xx level class. Had 6 projects, 6 quizzes, one midterm, and one final, plus a few attendance points. He recorded video lectures, but I learned more from reviewing the class notes and actually doing the projects, which were pretty though.

The lectures are fantastic, but the organization is truly horrendous. How does a professor forget to give a midterm? But the lectures are fantastic, I feel like I learned a lot from this course, and I absolutely do not regret taking it with Kruskal at all.

The professor does have some pretty bad anxiety at times and it can be really uncomfortable for the students, but overall he is a great professor. His explanations can be extremely in depth and hard to follow but he does not expect you to be able to derive those explanations for yourself, just to build some intuition as to why things work. His homework’s were pretty difficult but he would give out tips and answers when students were really struggling, his exams were extremely fair and very similar to his sample exams. I recommend taking this class with Dr Petersdorff.
she's pretty good at lecturing + pretty lenient too + assignments/exams are VERY fair. 10/10 recommend.

Cosigning the reviewer from 04/17/2025. This class is pretty much INST126 but more in-depth. Ironically, if you are taking the asynchronous section and aren't well versed in Python you may struggle a bit. However the general track of anything Computer Science related ends up being you having to teach yourself, especially what field you'd like to pursue. So don't think too hard about it, you should generally be fine. Patrick was a fantastic professor for this course and if he is teaching it at any time I'd highly recommend to take him. I'm also rehashing the common complaints with a lot of these coding classes: the instructions are generally unclear and too vague at times. I wish expectations of assignments were more clear-cut going forward but I understand there are different solutions to the same problem. Grading this semester were prompt and on time. Don't stress about being perfect with these assignments like I have, just focus on submitting something that satisfies the prompt or instructions.

Highly recommend taking him. Fantastic professor with good presentation. Lectures were more organized than before. Make sure you have solid group members for your project so you can get stuff done on time. Labs and general absence policies were very laid-back, you can practically take this class from home if you can. TAs can be a little frustrating in general, but other than that this class is generally easy mode. Definitely prepare to teach yourself mySQL for some assignments. Also personal advice: highly recommend putting the project you do for this course on your resume if you're pursuing any internships. It helps a lot.

Great guy, great professor! Honestly was expecting five star reviews on here when I checked and I was really surprised to see otherwise. Excellent professor if you're interested in data science, I really feel like I learned a lot in this class regarding bias/discrimination, and he does a great job of showing actual applications from his previous research. I actually felt like I left this class being able to do work that can have an impact.
Professor is super open to students, all work is reasonable and covered in lecture videos.
Exams are a little hard, he is very nice but he doesn't seem to care about teaching.

Dr. Ebrahimian was always willing to help his students, taking time to answer questions to ensure everyone understands. He is very organized in how he structured the class, to make no confusion with assignment submissions or exams. There are quizzes and worksheets due every week, but it holds you accountable so you have to understand the content. He is very clearly a knowledgeable guy, and is always happy to speak with students. His lectures are great and he likes to make funny jokes at times.
Very good professor, knows what he is talking about and doesn't rush anything, grades fairly, super nice guy

Always got the tuffest fits on and his tests are free lol. Curve is very generous, didn't go to lecture and just studied with chat. Also literally gave us the type of problems to expect on midterm 2 and the final (and you made your own cheatsheet for the final). Probably easiest STAT400 class ever, and you don't have to go to lecture

Dr. Khurana has to be the best math professor I've had so far! She's so kind and understanding, and ensures that all students have every resource possible to learn and succeed in her class. During lecture, she has a kind of "base" for her notes, which she works through with examples and more notes. She then posts these "updated" notes on canvas. These notes have everything you need to know about every topic, so if you miss something in class, you could just check on her notes and be up-to-date again. The exams are really similar to the class examples and practice exams, so as long as you review, you'll do well on them! She also took lots of student feedback throughout the course, such as when to hold in-class quizzes and whether she should hold a review session, which I appreciated a lot. I genuinely think that she sets up every student to succeed, and as long as you use the provided resources, you could do well in this course. My only feedback is that I wish there were more direction on the coding assignments, since some students may not have experience with coding, Python, or R, and we were only given the problems without any directions on how we should actually write the code. If you do have even a little coding experience, though, the projects are very straightforward.

3.5 stars, genuinely she isn't as bad as people say. Honestly, I feel her reviews are a little too harsh. Her slides are pretty basic, but (most) the material is very similar to AP CSA, where there is a LOT of review material online on. I think Nora is incredibly nice, and her TAs were helpful in holding review sessions, but I do agree that she is not the best person to explain every concept in a way that sticks and is thorough. I think navigating Nora's 131 is knowing your resources and practicing, which seems like a lot but once you get a routine it truly isn't hard, I promise. I did the projects early on and diligently, watched YT videos for concepts that were difficult, used ChatGPT to generate quick intuitive notes to read and some practice questions. Note: CHATGPT IS NOT FOR PROJECTS, THAT WOULD ONLY BE CHEATING YOURSELF, lots of projects had high averages and the exams... not so much, please use those projects to your advantage and study productively so you aren't cramming and barely practicing. She did not curve the exams but they were pretty similar to the practice test/question bank she gave out. Exam 2 was a little more challenging in that sense but if you understood the lecture, wasn't too crazy in difficulty and you could piece the difficult questions together. The final had a couple challenging questions but nothing too wild. What to really emphasis in your study is PRACTICE, that's the only way to learn how to intuitively code in this course and beyond. Lastly, her lectures. Mixed feelings about this. Her lectures were really boring and I could almost swear half the class was doing something else. But if you needed to revisit, she had them recorded. I honestly felt, even though I didn't pay much attention, the general idea sank in and then I self studied later. Looking back, I wish I paid attention so I could save some time, haha, but self studying using the slides and online resources got the job done. That being said, I do have solidly decent prior Java experience so it wasn't all that foreign to me. If you have never coded before, this could be a steep learning curve, but in that case just power through the boring 50 minute lecture, genuinely try your best to understand+practice, and you should be alright, believe in yourself :) TLDR: If you end up with Nora, it's not the worst. Make a diligent self-study schedule, stick to it, and practice using her material. utilize all possible resources. you will achieve your goals. ALL THE BEST
he's mid but good enough, explains content with depth so good if you have no prior knowledge

Nicole is the only reason why I am still alive in 216 w/ Yoon. She is super nice and helpful and I wish she was our lecturer because her explanations always make 100x more sense than those given by Yoon. She is goated

Lectures are fast paced and can be boring at times but attend them and PLEASE listen to him when he says "do the homework the day it's assigned". The homework is not graded so not mandatory but it's so helpful and if you ever have questions, you can go to OH and get help. Overall, wonderful person and a great lecturer. The exams weighting is a lot and small mistakes can lose you lots of points (how I ended with a B+) but I had friends end with A+ since they didn't make the silly mistakes I made. Just put effort and you'll pass easily. Overall wonderful lecturer for this class. 10/10 would recommend and take him again if I could.

Maks is a pretty interesting professor who brings up important ideas that make you think deeply about the topics during lecture. Unfortunately, this also extends to his approach to exams. Your grades on exams are not dictated by how well you study or pay attention to the lectures but instead by how well you understand data science. This may sound fair but when you apply that to an intro course, you are getting taught basic ideas and then expected to extrapolate from that like a career data scientist (he even takes questions from data science interviews). Every question on his exams is a trick question. These questions are often poorly worded (doesn't clearly indicate what it's looking for) or straight up impossible (he had to take a couple of these off the exams). This can be a fun challenge if you have a light semester, but if you have a really heavy schedule, it becomes a nightmare of bashing your brains against the material hoping something sticks. If you are thinking about being a data scientist, this is the course for you. Taking this course tests your resolve and tells you if you actually want to be a data scientist. I thought I wanted to be a data scientist but this course showed me that I had a bright future in creative writing. Although, after a semester of getting straight Cs on exams and bombing homeworks, I still ended up with a B so he's a pretty understanding grader.

Anwar is pretty good. Him and Cliff coteach so no difference as far as exams, projects, etc. He teaches really well imo when he goes off his slides, which is about half the time. And then the other half he just does random examples on emacs which can sometimes be helpful and other times just makes things confusing. But overall he is pretty solid.

Nelson as a person is great, but I’ve always he’d the belief that you retain little to no information through his courses, and that he gets majority 5 star reviews due to the fact that his classes and exams are so easy to pass. This problem is exacerbated in 335, which is a course that needs to be destroyed by the computer science department and rebuilt from the ground up. Easy A, bad class.

The absolute Michael Jordan of TAs. He knows this course inside and out, and could 100000% take it over himself. Without him, I would have been lost in the sauce. He is the sole reason why I willed myself to class every week. I am truly appreciative of him and his work throughout this semester, and highly recommend him not only as a TA, but as a role model.

She's a fine lecturer she's not bad but not good lectures are mainly her reading off slides. She records so that's a bonus. The workload composes of just three homeworks three projects one final and one midterm. Overall probably the best computer system architecture professor right now but the only other option is yoon so that's not really a high bar. This wasn't a hard class but also not very exciting average on the midterms were a 73+ if you did the homeworks and projects you could easily get a B+ or higher. To be honest she's more of a four star professor but because your only option right now as of the time of writing this review is her or yoon that automatically makes her a five star professor in my opinion because she is one in comparison.

Ashok's not good at lecturing. Exams are very difficult. I would prep around 30+ hours and take notes on every chapter of textbook and I got around 70, 90, 80 on M1, M2, Final respectively. Projects are all doable, but take a long time... especially for debugging. The harder projects can take 20+ hours. Also, information about the project is scattered across a project spec, slides provided by the TA, and project overview discussions sections (which are not recorded). Make sure to go to discussion on days they introduce new projects. Make sure to start as early as possible so you can go to OH. The TAs carry the course. Overall, your grade in this class mostly comes down to how much time you can spend on the class. I only took 3 classes this semester, and spent a lot of time for this class. The grade is split between (1) projects ~40, (2) two exams ~30, (3) final ~25, (4) participation ~5. No insight into how participation grade works, but projects can really help to boost your grade if you do them all on time :). I ended with an 89, and this was curved to an A+

His lectures were pretty engaging and he's clearly interested in the content, but the disorganization of the class left a lot to be desired. Stuff doesn't get graded for a long time, like one project that took over a month to be graded. The final ended up online with little warning. His grading was also messed up for the final, which he had to correct (to his credit, he did fix it). The last project was a partner project and my partner wasn't added to the gitlab for an entire 2 weeks, despite the emails he ignored. I like his lectures, but I wouldn't take him again due to the lack of care he puts into the administration of the class.

Pros: - Having seven exams means that each exams only has two or three data structures on it, so that makes studying a bit easier. I feel like one thing I struggled with in 351 was trying to keep all of the algorithms straight, and I liked having fewer topics on each exam. - Justin is very receptive to feedback and adapts based on the needs of students. He decided to drop a second exam because people asked for it on Piazza. I am guessing he will do some restructuring of the course based on reviews - In my personal opinion, the exams were not unfairly challenging. I am NOT one of those super smart cs kids (far from it) but I got As and Bs on all of the exams. A lot of people didn't do well on the first exam, I think because it came so early in the semester and it had a few really difficult high-point-value problems. He changed the exams as the semester went on, so the rest of them were mostly short questions with one long-form question at the end. Cons: - Not having any homeworks means your grade is composed of only projects and exams. However, he does drop your lowest exam and lowest project so I don't think that is necessarily the end of the world. - Projects were ROUGH. He lists 3 and 5 as the "hard" projects but I thought project 4 was just as bad. I would spend upwards of 30 hours trying to make my code work. Overall I would recommend this class for a CS elective and Justin as a professor. I think he puts a lot of effort into curating a good class experience and will continue to improve on the things that made 420 a rough experience for some people.

Dr. Kim and Dr. Regli were co-teaching this semester (Fall 2025), so their lectures, homework, projects, and exams were the same. I think you should probably have some basic background in AI because I didn't, so that made all the concepts really hard to understand/follow. But this is a skill issue lol Some notes: - 3 coding projects. ACTUALLY DO PROJECT 1 WELL BEFORE THE DUE DATE PLEASE 🙏🙏🙏 It is the hardest project out of all 3. Even if they haven't taught the concepts yet, just use Google and stuff to learn, JUST DO IT EARLY!!!! All projects are coding + writing. For example, for Project 1, you had to write a full report alongside the code. - 4 homeworks. - 2 midterms and 1 final (non-cumulative). You're allowed a cheatsheet (front and back) for all exams. All exams are multiple choice, so no partial credit. - All lectures are recorded. - All slides are posted. - Optional 1-2 hour recitations/discussions where TAs or the professors explain some of the concepts or how to start a project. In my opinion, midterms 1 and 2 were too close together (I think they were a little over a month apart), but maybe my perception of time was warped lol. In either case, the content needed for the final feels like a whole year's worth of content with how dense it is. So don't be fooled by the "non-cumulative"; the final will always be hard for a conceptually challenging class like this one. Dr. Regli is an okay guy. His hats are fun. I haven't spoken to him one-on-one or asked for help during office hours, but I think he lectures okay...? The way he explains things can sometimes be contradictory and not that well-explained. I think to really understand his lectures, you have to read the book (optional), research/learn on your own, and review a lot. Piazza is not the greatest place to get clear answers. Dr. Regli tends to get a bit annoyed when students ask the same question, which is fair since there is a search bar in Piazza, but sometimes his answers to questions can come off as a bit condescending. It is kind of funny when he types out "sigh" though...

Given my past experience with Professor Teli in CMSC250 being largely positive, overall I found CMSC422 to be really rather disappointing. First off, the class was extremely disorganized in most ways; projects had faulty/incorrect code, test questions were rather vague, and Piazza questions were often left somewhat unanswered. For one of the projects that had extra credit, the grading on ELMS kept being changed to include and exclude extra credit, which overall made it really confusing. It was extremely frustrating especially how tests were made, as often the wording of questions led to me getting things wrong annoyingly. Although the exams have a cheat sheet, sometimes the questions went over rather obscure topics or sections of the material, which could often come by surprise. I did not like how Teli lectured at all. Most of the time, Teli goes over a slideshow and writes notes and derivations for algorithms and models on paper. Teli often writes his math extremely quickly, without any structure and rather unsorted, so it was often really difficult to understand the material that was being gone over. Yes, the material overall is complex, but it felt like concepts that shouldn't be too difficult were obfuscated by how Teli taught it. What Teli teaches also feels rather disconnected from what the tests have as a whole. It felt that lectures really only vaguely helped with the test's material, and I felt there was a lack of questions/assignments that gave us more practice answering questions that could appear on tests. From talking with people who had Teli in the past, there was a rather large difference in grades between different semesters (75% average this semester vs 95% average last semester on Exam 1). It's overall quite frustrating that despite this, little was done to reconcile the differences in scores (there was a 1% curve admittedly, but it was still honestly not a lot). I guess to talk about some positives, there was extra credit for one of the projects and all lectures were recorded luckily. And compared to some of the reviews for the other CMSC422 professors this semester, Teli may still be one of the better options. Still though, I found that this class frustrated me more than not, and I ended up getting very little from this class overall.

This was the hardest CMSC4xx class I've taken, but this is the most I've learned in a CS class at UMD. Abadi is an incredibly knowledgeable professor and wants you to learn. I enjoyed the projects quite a bit, from mastering SQL to writing a B+ tree in Java. Both TAs were also great and put a ton of work into answering Piazza questions and providing support during the projects. Yes, this class is hard and requires a ton of investment to learn the material. There are graded clicker questions each class and exams are extremely difficult (Abadi likes to say getting questions wrong is another form of learning the material). The midterm was curved by about 15%. I've heard that Herve teaches an easier version of the course. However, if you have the time and put in the effort, take it with Abadi and I guarantee you will walk away from this class with so much knowledge applicable to software engineering.

Took him Spring 2025. First quiz, first exam, and project 5 had harsh distributions, but besides that the class was pretty forgiving. Projects were heavily weighted and time consuming, so I recommend starting early. Overall, no complaints - he's a funny guy who has an odd teaching style (literally just writes code in emacs the whole time and rarely opens his slides), but if you are choosing between him and Cliff, I'd recommend Anwar because his exams seemed to be easier than Cliffs this semester (even though the exams are roughly the same across all sections).

Bro just don't take this class. Anwar's a nice person and is pretty accommodating & teaches concepts pretty well, but the material is just kind of ass and projects are confusing. Please don't take this class if you don't like proofs... I honestly have no idea why I even decided to take this one and it was one hell of a ride. There are 6 projects, a midterm, and a final. It's just too much. I thought the final was going to be simple enough but it really wasn't :( Projects build on top of each other so if you don't understand concepts you better fix that earlier in the semester.

Dave Mount is easily the best professor I’ve ever had. First off, he’s an awesome lecturer–no matter the complexity of the algorithm, proof, NP-reduction or whatever concept it is, Mount always manages to explain it and break it down until it’s totally intuitive. He’s also just a really nice guy. You can ask him really anything about the course material or homework and he’ll happily give you more information than you even needed and he never makes you feel like you asked a dumb question. With that in mind, I CANNOT recommend attending his office hours enough. The homework problems can get really challenging, but if you go to OH, he’s always willing to help lead you in the right direction, or quickly look through your solution and provide general feedback. The exams are admittedly kind of brutal. They were both 2 hours, but devising and writing out a description, proof of correctness, and running time of an algorithm takes so long that there’s simply not enough time to fully think over each question–you just have to see the solution immediately or you won’t be able to finish the exam. HOWEVER, Mount is an insanely generous grader, so even if you don’t see how to answer an algorithm question, he offers so much partial credit (more than I felt like I deserved) if you demonstrate even some knowledge of the base concepts. This class is really challenging and you will need to dedicate a lot of time to it, but I’ve learned so much and the help/resources Mount provides are more than enough to help you succeed.

Class extremely easy but if you choke any assignment or test its over for you. I suspect that class will be good class when she gets firmer grasp on what content should be and what assignments/tests to give. Knowledgable person I think. For now, pretty bad but easy upper level.
Aric is by far my favorite professor at UMD. Incredibly smart and great guy. Take his class.

The class is fine. You can't go wrong with taking him, but there's also nothing really crazy to say about him. The TAs are a little too harsh on grading, but that's in part due to his rubric. You don't end up learning much databases; things are easy enough to just not go to lecture and learn off the videos in a few hours. Seems pleasant, though!

If you take this professor, you better pay attention in his class. He might randomly call on you and you’ll be set up for humiliation. This guy seems to really enjoy putting students on the spot and embarrassing them

Avoid this professor. Very knowledgeable about what he teaches, but this class is all over the place. The instructional team has had to constantly push back due dates because of mistakes or just not releasing the assignment until 2 or 3 days before the due date. literally the best teacher ever. she makes concepts super understandable and the way she structured the course was really helpful for students. there's a quiz almost every week, but the question is taken directly from the homework (and homework isn't graded/submitted - you only do it to be ready for the quiz). the worksheets aren't difficult and can be done in groups. all the questions in the midterms are extremely similar to worksheet/homework/quiz questions, so you definitely want to go through all the material to be prepared. although the final is made by chadwick, her class prepares you well enough for it. i'm just sad she wasn't here to teach math141 in spring 26.

Super good lecturer who genuinely cares. Quizzes are much easier than the exams, although the homework does take a while. Exams are pretty hard, but he gives a list of suggested problems on Canvas. If you put in the work and do all of them, it prepares you very well for the exam because he'll make a lot of the problems very similar to the suggested problems. Also, I once dropped my keycard in class and he drove all the way to North Campus to return it to me :) very kind

If you're taking linear algebra, I highly recommend that you DO NOT take this professor. Taking this class was draining; I studied so much to end with a B+. The concepts in this class aren't hard, but the tests he gives make it hard, and honestly, it is better to have a worse lecturer who gives easier exams. Lastly, his grade distributions on ELMS are wrong, and he purposefully announces it on the week of finals, when there is nothing you can do about it. Make sure to calculate your grade using the syllabus distributions and DON'T trust the score automatically calculated by ELMS.

He's not a very good lecturer, and his notes are confusing to read. The quizzes are pretty simple and the exams are okay since he posts the practice problems. But reviewing the practice problems is honestly the only way to learn the material, I wouldn't say he really taught anything effectively. He seems understanding though.

I would give negative stars if I could. His rating is not accurate because someone gave 5 stars to inflate the rating. No structure at all in the course, his slides were terrible and the practice problems he gave never correlated with what we were learning so we had no idea how to do them. If you are a cs major, Kyeongwon Lee is the alternate stat version of Kruskal (not as bad tho). Only upside is that he is a nice person. Not worth it. BE ADVISED.

Overall great guy and a chill professor. The class has a ton of work, but he provides so many resources to study. Make sure to review old topics for each exam so your coding stays up to date. he records lectures and is extremely nice.

Hermann was probably the most mid professor out there. He's not bad, but not good. The class is extremely boring, and he threatens you to show up with pop quizzes, though a majority of them are in discussion, which don't have his no technology rule. he also takes forever to grade, I had maybe 4 grades in total until after the final.
