If you're confident in 132 content, I would avoid.

If you haven't already, go look at that rating and the amount of reviews. On god it is not a lie, he deserves it. When I tell you his class will be a detriment to your mental health and academic career I'm not joking. I'm going break down why though: 1. His teaching style is to essentially overload you with a bunch of information, most of which isn't relevant for the upcoming task such as project or test/quizzes. So while you're busy trying to sift through what you need and don't, along with trying to understand the topic at hand, he's already moved on to the next. Which is infuriating because I'm paying thousands of dollars for this to be my experience. 2. Remember what I said about this unnecessary things he'll teach in class? Yeah he'll make those small things important questions on his test/quizzes. 3. He will, and I mean will, overload you with work. The best way to put it, he operates as if his class is the only one you're taking. To give you an example, literally the night of our first exam, he assigned the next coding project and told us "I suggest you get started on this immediately". I got the notification for the assignment literally late night while me and a friend were studying for HIS exam that was going to happen later that day in Mckeldin. As you can image we were pissed. And he also gives little-to-no time between projects to breath. 4. Speaking of the projects, his project documents are longwinded and vague. So much so that the piazza is littered with people asking for clarification on things that should be crystal clear constantly. And you can get a bunch of points docked if you miss just 1 of the several details he gives you in his, on average, 7 page docs. Which if you ask me, it makes no sense that you have a doc that long and people in droves are still asking for basic clarification. You wrote all that for nothing then. 5. The TAs are hit or miss, and it's almost dramatic. Some are really cool and helpful, while others feel as if they think just being there while offering little to no should guarantee them a check. I had to hassle one of them to tell me what was wrong with my code for like an hour as I obviously didn't know and tried almost everything at that point. And once they finally helped me, it took them like 10 minutes to find the issue and relay it to me. There has also been multiply times where TAs will change their hours without updating the google calendar, and as a commuter it's just rage inducing. And I've brought this to Yoon's attention before and he acts as if it's a trivial matter. Like bro I'm wasting gas and time and he's so tight with his deadlines it makes no sense that he's chill about this. (Now the TA thing isn't that important since they're subject to change, but considering he chooses who becomes his TA, I think it's still worth mentioning). 6. His late policy. I don't think it's bad but I think it's worth mentioning and from here you can decide whether you're cool with it. So essentially you can turn in a assignment late only 24 hours after it's initial due date. So if it wad due the 21st at 11pm (yes all his projects are due at 11 pm, not 11:59pm), then the late due date is the 22nd at 11pm. And he will reduce the overall grade for this assignment by 15%. But don't get this confused with the GFA requirements, where if you don't meet them for each project you will be dropped by a letter grade. You can go back for any project to meet the GFA requirements (which could be to just pass all public test for example), but you won't get a new grade for that assignment. So if you get a 75% on that project, that's what you're stuck with. In all, please just avoid his class. It's unnecessary stress and I'd recommend that you don't pair this class with cmsc250. Take one or the other, especially if you can't escape his class for whatever reason (like me). And sure he has a seemingly nice personality and all, but if he was truly as nice as people say I don't think he'd work his students to the bone the way he does. It's needless and truly from my experience, I won't be able to say with confidence that I know how to code C by the end of this class since I and many others just understand enough to get the projects out of our faces and to get barely passing grades on his quizzes and exams. So if you want to actually know what you're doing, don't take him. GOOD LUCK!

Decent TA, could greatly improve with managing many students and ensuring that everyone gets equal time/attention. Okay, he's a very divisive professor. I think the upshot is that if you're genuinely passionate about the material, you'll absolutely find him to be a 5/5. If you just want an easy time, take Fardina. I don't know exactly. I'm not sure how much of an impact it had because I feel as though we got through most if not all the material we needed to, but it did mean he had to throw out a project. I can understand where his bad reviews come from... but I personally found this to be an easy class, and absolutely think that he deserves a much higher rating (2.8 at time of writing). One of my favorite professors, if not my absolute favorite.

Here is the thing, he really just isn't that good of a lecturer. He can be very disorganized, and he can forget to share vital information unless a student explicitly asks. I think his exams/projects were pretty fair. His projects can be a bit tough, but they certainly help you prepare for the exams so make sure to spend time on them.

I also took 216 with Nelson and have never really been a fan of his teaching style. I just find it easy to become disengaged with how often he goes off topic. However, he's an extremely kind professor who cares a lot about his students. This class in specific is extremely easy to get an A in as long as you make sure you follow the instructions for all projects and set aside a day or 2 to "study" for the exams (just memorize the format). He is an excellent professor who puts genuine effort into explaining algorithmic concepts clearly and provides decent learning resources. His lectures are engaging, he communicates effectively and maintains the class’s attention without being monotonous. However, his exams and homework assignments can be quite difficult, and his grading tends to be strict. He places strong emphasis on understanding and accurately tracing his pseudocode for algorithms. Overall, the course is challenging, striking a balance that makes it a rewarding learning experience.

She's very smart and knows what she's talking about, but it's hard to understand what she's talking about a lot of the time. Her slide shows also don't help much, they don't explain a lot of the details that matter for the homework and exams. The workload is pretty light, just 3 homeworks, 3 projects, and 1 midterm and final. But the homeworks have some poorly worded questions that are hard to understand what they're asking. Overall, not a bad teacher but you have to really like computer architecture to enjoy the class at all. It's also memorization heavy for the exams.

CMSC412 with Ashok was difficult. I was forced to enter this class as there were no other CS classless to take to fulfill my last reqs to graduate. I was very worried because this class was known to be difficult and if I didn't pass that would've caused all sorts of issues for me. For those students who are in Cs get degrees mode, you can get a C, you just will have to work very hard for it. The exams and projects are difficult. The projects are 40% of the class grade, if you go to office hours religiously the TAs can help you get unstuck fairly quickly. This way your project grades will be your saving grace even if you were bombing the exams like I was. There is a test bank that you can use to practice for them, they are found on neil's CS home page, google cmsc 412 home page and dig around you will find it. There were questions from tests from 1996 that were pasted onto our exams. So, if you don't want to try very hard to pass, and you don't like OS, don't take this class. If you need to pass this class and you are a bit of a bum, then you need to do well in the projects, the office hours and recitations will help you and then you don't have to do incredible on the exams to pass. Those people who did not pass were the people who did poorly on the projects AND the tests. To pass this class you must choose between the projects or the exams to do poorly in. It is easer to do poorly on the exams, the projects despite their difficulty, if you use OFFICE HOURS ALOT, you will do well on them and do better than the rest of the class. If you are wondering about a curve, or how the grading scheme is, Ashok seemed to be purposely unclear about curves or grading schemes. But for my class, he must've had a generous curve based on me passing with my class grade of 68% +/- the final ( one person passed with a 63% +/- the final) , we aren't quite sure how big the curve is because he never told anyone how they did on the final that was around 30% of the grade (hence the +/-).

On the plus side, his exams were fairly easy in comparison to my other classes, and his projects do an okay job of scaling in difficulty. Speaking to the class as a whole: There is WAY too much content. It feels as though you scratch the surface level of 20 different concepts, and come out having really learned nothing.

The lectures were very engaging, well organized, and easy to follow. I enjoyed the course structure of breaking the topics into exams every 2 weeks. Each exam only required reviewing a small amount of material, and we dropped the lowest exam grade. My only qualm is that we didn’t go too deep into the theory behind a lot of the data structures. There were a lot of times where it seemed like Justin held back from material that may have been a bit challenging, which limited how much I learned from the course. Most proof questions on homeworks/exams were minor variants of proofs done in class.

Regli is fantastic- I can't understand the hate. He updates the slides regularly, exams are fair and you even get a cheat sheet. To do poorly in this course you have to try. He's extremely knowledgeable and funny with great lectures that make you think and content that is worth connecting to.

Teli's just kind of an average CS professor, "not too hot, not too cold". He posts lecture slides, though they almost certainly cannot support all of your learning in the course, since they are a bit incoherent (maybe that's the point of the lectures). He gives practice exams before each exam, and he and his TAs were fairly active on Piazza. I thought his exams were fair and generally alright, but the grading could be a bit harsh at times (on the midterm, there was a question with no partial credit at all, worth 20% of that exam's grade). He gave HWs roughly biweekly, which we had two attempts at in case you missed anything the first time. Moreover, there were three coding projects, each had a "writeup" portion (worth up to 40% of the project's grade) where you'd have to answer conceptual questions on the code and sometimes provide graphs. Not to mention, these projects did not have an autograder! Overall, I am not upset having taken the course with Teli—I just wish both of the professors for this class were better, since this class could be so interesting if there was someone engaging who taught it.

Herve is super friendly, like genuinely one of the nicest guys at UMD. I overslept for a quiz once and I emailed him asking if there was anything I could do, and because he's so kind he just let me make it up with a small penalty. On top of that he gave me chances to submit the right assignment, and hes just a good teacher in general so I would recommend.
Pierce is more responsible than DVH and is the most helpful TA I’ve ever had in a CS course. Dude responds to Piazza posts at 1am in 5-10 minutes. What else can I say?

Do NOT take 433, especially with him. It is about program validation, not concurrent programming, and it's a pretty useless class in my opinion. He is a really nice professor, but they added a final exam because he realized everyone is using AI for the projects. His lectures are really boring, and he usually confuses himself and the class because he messes up syntax when copying code from his notes in class. His online notes were way more helpful than his lectures.

Mount is an incredible professor. I'd argue that Mount is just as good or better than Justin at teaching and visualizing concepts. He has handwritten notes and typed up notes to reference and goes through his handwritten notes in class since it is pre-written. I would recommend listening and jotting down only important facts to not fall behind in lecture. Additionally, his lectures are recorded but I would recommend going to class since it is easier to understand the topics when listening in person. The content of this class is dense and difficult and there is a homework assigned every two weeks with roughly 5 problems. These problems take a long time since there are proofs and explanations so do not wait until the last minute to do them. I would also recommend doing the extra credit problems. There is one midterm and a final. The exams were tough but Mount does not grade harshly. The class consists of various algorithms and NP-reductions which was very interesting. This class felt like the most "real" CS course I have taken so far. Mount is an engaging lecturer and is very kind. He is perhaps one of the best professors I have ever taken so I'd highly recommend taking this class with Mount.

The first half of this class was pretty good - lectures were clear, assignments and midterm were very fair. But then all of a sudden it's like she stopped caring after the midterm. No homework or practice problems whatsoever on like half of the course material (that too, the more difficult half). No responses to most Piazza questions. No one knows how to prepare for the final, and it's worth 45% of the overall grade. Most of us are just hoping for a heavy curve at this point. The one good thing I can say is that she's a kind and understanding person, even if disorganized. Overall, I'd say take this course with another professor if possible, you'll learn more and probably be less stressed.
Professor is easy in terms of if you can teach yourself you are fine. He does not grade the final project btw ! so whatever ur grade is before the final project that is your grade

Really chill guy and an easy class overall. Just put the time in to understand SQL and you'll breeze through his assignments and labs. They're easy. I stopped going to lecture after a few weeks since I can look at his lecture notes/videos and refer to the textbook. The group project isn't difficult by any means but just hope to have good group members. I highly recommend him.

Chill, reasonable guy who gets straight to the point with the course content. I enjoyed taking 414 with him. The content is high-level, but you will be allowed access to AI resources and will walk through the technicals in class.

Would not recommend. I'm usually not the type to complain about professors but this class is not well taught at all. His auto grader assignments has errors and his due date time is jank. On top of all of that, his test covers content that the hw didn't even cover yet. I'm not exaggerating, hw 4 was not even due until the day after the test, yet he tested us on content that's covered in hw 5.

Amazing teacher. Explains everything super well and is easy to understand. She made calculus easy (this was my first-ever time taking calc). Homeworks were great (optional, but very helpful for practice). One worksheet and one quiz per week, during class discussions. Worksheets were for working in groups, and they made comprehension of the material a lot easier. The quizzes were one question each and were easy if you had kept up with worksheets/homework. Exams were exactly as she described, and you'll ace them if you practice the homework problems. Honestly, I have no complaints. The material wasn't the easiest, considering it was my first time, but this professor made it a great first experience. I HIGHLY recommend taking her. I WISH I could take her for math141 but she's going on maternity leave (congrats!!). Thank you Prof S.!!
Don't take him, ridiculous make-up policy, never checks emails, incredibly hard tests. Only upside is his lectures are interesting. Good luck communicating with him outside of lectures.

Shin Song is a really great professor who provides a lot of resources to help you succeed in her class. The class consists of weekly quizzes (every Tuesday and only on Thursdays if it is after an exam week), 3 midterms, 2 MATLABS, and a final. She uploads her notes after every lecture. Her quizzes are super easy to get 100% as she just tells you what kind of problems are going to be on the quiz, and the TA also goes over similar problems right before the quiz in discussion. She gives out 2 practice exams before every midterm, and they are similar to what the midterms would actually look like. Her grading is really lenient on exams. The MATLABs are super easy and free points. She also dropped the two lowest quizzes and the lowest MATLAB.

I think I'm of the minority opinion but I thought his lecture style was ok. You definitely need to put some time outside of class to understand the content though. Quizzes are super easy and I think the midterms were fair, but other people definitely have different opinions. The final is 40% of our final grade and it was absolute hell, but he gave us a gigantic curve so we all wound up getting a higher grade than expected. He's a prof will actually curve, which I can't say about like any of my math or cs professors I've had so far. Very nice dude who cares about your GPA, but don't expect the lectures to be enough to actually understand what's happening.
Archana Khurana is a very solid professor. A very fair person (too fair) makes the classes a breeze. Cannot complain. Also seems to be a nice person. Will recommend any class taught by the goat.

Prof Aaron is a kind and funny guy. But if you come into this class with zero CS knowledge, you're cooked. What he goes over in lecture and teaches is NOTHING like his midterms. He gives past exams/practice exams, but again NOTHING like the midterms, so it's like you're wasting your time doing them. Whereas other professors make their midterms fair and based on the class material. He is also VERY slow with grading, and it's often impossible to know what you have in the class until the very end, and there's no way of predicting your grade cause he doesn't post all the assignments on Canvas. I highly recommend taking a different professor if you do not have background Java knowledge, because this class was insane. If you do end up having to take him, please go to office hours and do not fall behind. My TA helped me a lot, and I wouldn't have ended up with the grade I wanted without her. However, I am still giving him 3 stars because he was nice enough to round my 92.36 to a 93.

His lectures and slides were very good. The projects are extremely detailed and very useful for understanding the content. Make sure to go to every lecture and discussion because getting a 0 on a graded worksheet will heavily decrease your grade. Note that he does not allow students to use any devices during class, but this shouldn't be a big issue if you manage your time effectively outside of class.

He's quirky but a great lecturer (not a professor). Our exam Averages were lower than Kaufman who was teaching 216 at the same time, which is something to keep in mind. But imo the exams were generally difficult, but fair and he gives you a lot of resources to prepare for them ahead of time.

i'm decently lukewarm about teli. - his lecturing gave you the bare minimum in what you needed to know for hw and quizzes. his lectures can be a little wishy-washy within explanations - hw, discussion and quizzes were harder than the examples covered in lecture. had to spend a lot of time in OH figuring this out - exams were easy compared to the hw/discussions/quizzes. this is a redeaming quality of the class - TAs were a mess, regularly skipping OH, each TA would give you different answers to the same hw questions, partially like this because teli does not provide answer keys or grading guidelines to TAs - generally proof notes were sloppy, it makes it hard to figure out what is syntaxtically acceptable for an exam. grading felt random at times - recordings were a nice to have overall he is an okay professor, he get's the job done. 250 is generally taught a little bit confusingly, so if you're not a math person, plan to spend extra time in OH to figure this class out.

I had the 2 PM lecture for this class, and it was the best decision I've ever made. His lectures are entertaining at times, and he's probably one of the funniest professors here at UMD. But I honestly don't think he should be teaching at all. He has a great knowledge of data science, but this was a class I was really looking forward to taking, and was really interested in the content, but Max, as the professor, was a big no. He doesn't know how to teach and is probably one of the laziest professors here. His exams are pretty hard, and he doesn't help you with review. He posts these like weekly recaps, but they are kind of useless because they are vague about what you should know. His practice exams are nothing close to his actual exams, so they are just useless. Homeworks were not that hard, and he gave a lot of time to complete them, which was great. But honestly, I barely learned anything from him and really had to teach myself everything. Max is a great guy, but he is not suited to be a professor.

Look as a person this guy is great he is funny and has good interaction with his students. However, he may be one of the worst lecturers I have had in terms of learning comprehension. Most of the slides are not in order to his material and often he transitions into examples that sure are useful but then take up a lot of time. As a result theory is much less covered which is a large issue for a class based heavily in it

This class is honestly a joke. You really don’t need to go to lecture at all because you can teach yourself everything. Each project took me maybe 2–3 hours max, and for the exams, you just need to study the day before. And by “study,” I mean memorize the format of the previous exams. I'm giving Nelson a 3 because he doesn’t seem very invested in what he’s teaching and tends to go off-topic a lot (another reason I skipped lectures. I didn’t feel like I learned much from them). I took this class alongside 330 and 351, and it wasn’t too much work overall.

This is my first time ever writing a review, but DO NOT TAKE HIS CLASS. You will find out midterm topics a week before the exam, if he even tells you when they are. Get ready to just learn through super old videos, but if you can manage learning through just those you should be okay. But no he's actually the worst so avoid at all costs.

Bahar is a very nice and knowledgeable professor. I would consider this course to be an intersection between computer engineering and science. You will go pretty far down into understanding different parts of a computer and how they work, right above the transistor level. Due to the low-level nature of this course, all of the projects are "simulation" rather than "development". (You aren't gonna build your own CPU pipeline lol). It relates to much more analysis of how different parts perform under different scenarios. They aren't very difficult imo. The exams are fair but are above average in difficulty imo. The difficulty isn't exactly hard because of the content, but because of the limited amount of time you have to finish. Work fast! This course is very content-dense; there is a lot of information that you have to learn. It can be easy to get lost in the sauce many times. Lectures are recorded, and they were an enormous help for reviewing material.

The projects are extremely time-consuming and it can be hard to figure out what to do since the project descriptions are vague sometimes and specific instructions are scattered across the project slides, project specification document, and random Piazza FAQ sections posted by the TAs. Agrawala himself has almost nothing to do with the projects; the TAs are pretty much your only help. The exams were difficult, but that's just the nature of CMSC412, so I can't blame Agrawala too much. The syllabus didn't describe the percent that each assignment contributed towards our grade, so we were left guessing the weight of each one. We also didn't get our final back, so we have no idea how well we did, let alone what questions we got right or wrong. Lectures are a complete snoozefest, but Agrawala can be quite funny sometimes. The only saving grace is that there is probably a decent curve, so you'll probably pass.

Pros: Great lecturer, he loves this content and makes lecture very engaging. I found the course content very interesting and relevant. The projects were fun to implement, and the exams were not unreasonably difficult Cons He's basically unreachable outside of class. And the TAs aren't helpful because he doesn't tell them anything. The Piazza was rarely helpful. I you have a serious question or concern about a grade - good luck. Grading takes forever.

It seems like Justin might change the class format in the next semester, so this only really applies if it is the 7 exam format. This class is honestly the overachiever in CS's dream class. Two out of seven exams are dropped, which means even if you have a bad exam a couple of times, you will still be alright. The final is online and is very easy, especially if you organize notes beforehand. I am not very good at coding, and I found all of the projects to be somewhat approachable (I skipped the B Tree one, however). He posts about 13ish practice problems before every exam that very closely model the exam format. No homework is required, so if you spend a good amount of time reviewing these problems, you will do well on the exam. The median in the class was a 90, so the average student who puts in effort will do alright. The tests are very easy because they are focused on such a small amount of material. You essentially have to understand ~2 - 3 different data structures for each test, and if you do, then you'll be golden. Justin's notes are amazing and provide you with all the information that you need to do well on exams. The only exception to this I would say is the skip lists exam as it is a lot more math heavy than the other exams.
i'm not sure how he is for normal semesters, but cmsc421 over the summer with him was very poorly run

The one star reviews some it up. The class itself wasn't hard and the material is interesting but she makes the exams too hard and teaches at too high of a conceptual level. Averages were really low and she didn't curve. Avoid taking at all costs !

Great Professor, I had him for both CMSC424 and 436. As long as you show up to class to understand lecture (the videos can be a little hard to understand sometimes), pay attention, do the HWs (which are very straightforward), and study for quizzes and exams ahead of time, you will most likely get an A. The content you need to know is straight from the slides, nothing ever is there to trick you. Sometimes if he makes the midterm too easy, he might give a harder quiz, but it all balances out. The projects in 424 specifically can be pretty cool to do when you get to coding, the HWs are fairly straightforward too

Took this course over the Summer with Anwar. It's same old Anwar, I'm not a huge fan of the way he teaches, but I also don't typically go to lecture, so it's not something too important to me. This course in particular tends to be taught identically regardless of professor because they're based off some really amazing notes written by someone whose name I cannot seem to find written down anywhere. If you're comfortable with assembly from 216, and the concepts from 330, you'll do quite well in this class from the notes alone. Since it was the Summer, it was nothing but projects and a few easy quizzes. Even the midterms were just projects. We weren't able to do the actual final, because Anwar only had classes 3 days a week instead of all 5, meaning we weren't able to cover all the content. We just did the next project as the final instead, so it was incredibly easy but still weighted disproportionately towards our grade. Regardless though, it was an interesting class, and besides having to join the Zoom each day (since he took attendance through Zoom polls) it was pretty easy, even if you're not listening to a word he says. If you like the way Anwar teaches, or if you're very comfortable with writing in assembly, working with parsing and interpreting, and don't mind learning from the (quite comprehensive) notes, then definitely take this class if it interests you.

Do NOT take Anwar for 433. The projects are not well timed, he is a boring lecturer who just refers to his online notes verbatim to teach, and has assigned projects over break and makes them due the same day as an exam. The one thing that I can say about the class is that it is well structured and that he does provide notes, but other professors who have taught 433 before have done a better job at making notes than he has. Very disappointing to experience this considering the nice reviews I have seen and heard from other classmates.

Truly an amazing professor. His lectures are super useful, he clearly cares about his students a lot, and he is a super nice guy. CMSC451 is a super difficult class. - Did you think the exams or other major assignments were fair? Homework is tough and takes a LOT of time, so get started on it early--you will learn a TON from these homeworks. Go to office hours to ask about the homeworks, he will lead you in the right direction. There are only 2 exams, a midterm and a final. Exams are challenging but fair. As long as you attempt a question, you will usually get some partial credit (try not to ever leave anything blank). Lock in early, i was caught off guard by the difficulty of the midterm and got a 61% which made things pretty tough. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- - Did you think the professor had reasonable expectations of the students in the course overall? Although challenging, I believe anyone can succeed in this class if they give a lot of effort. - Were you a fan of the professor's teaching style? I made the mistake early on of skipping a lot of class and just watching the lecture recordings. DONT do that. Going to lectures in person is suuper beneficial. He pre-handwrites his notes and talks about it pretty fast, so pay attention. He posts recordings, handwritten notes, and more formal typeset notes, which is nice. He is a really good teacher and has a way of explaining complex things that just make sense. - Was the workload appropriate for the number of credits? I think this class should be 4 credits. - Was this course a waste of time or was it beneficial in some way? By far the most interesting and most educational course I have ever taken. I would highly recommend to anyone even slightly interested in algorithms. My favorite topic was reductions and np completeness. This was the first class that actually made me feel like a computer "scientist". - How much support were you given throughout the semester (office hours, extra resources, etc.)? No discussion sessions, but there are a ton of office hour slots which were really helpful. Try to drop in and get help on homework.
Reads off slides. Very few assignments. Inactive on Piazza. Final worth 45% of your final grade.

Great man and a decent teacher !!! He did sometimes give out a lot of work but he also granted extensions if you asked him and if your reason complies with the syllabus. Would recommend this teacher if you are ready to do a lot of work..

DO NOT TAKE THIS CLASS!! As others have said assignment instructions were confusing and inconsistent. They would change on a whim with little to no prior notice and send half the class into a frenzy on disallowed terms (which were literally taught in the textbook). And, as everyone else has also mentioned she took the time to report half the class for cheating which severely impacted my mental health last semester. Imagine worry about your academics and then all of a sudden being accused of cheating (which i didn’t do and was eventually cleared of) which puts you into a 2 month long limbo period. That was easily the most stressful point in my life and I’m sure other students who also did nothing felt the same.
The class wasn't too hard, and we could turn in projects late and still get full points. Using ChatGPT made the projects much easier to complete.

sucks, uses autograder for assignments but his solutions aren't correct so he has to send out 3 announcements to tell you how to specifically overcome his idiosyncratic errors and vague solutions by adding specific lines of code and so you can arrive at his erroneous solution

Dr. S is a great math professor! I definitely recommend taking her class. She uses goodnotes to write on a pdf note sheet in class which is very helpful. She also uploads a blank version of the note sheet before lecture so you can follow along and take your own notes in class. She posts the lecture notes which are very detailed and include all of the steps so it is easy to catch up if you miss lecture. The homework was very helpful because the quizzes and exams use very similar problems to the homework. I also found going to her office hours to be very helpful, she always answered my questions thoroughly. The final exam was harder than the midterm exams but as long as you do well throughout the semester you will be prepared for the final.

Absolute goat. I did pretty poorly on the first 2 midterms and then reached out to him for help, and he did everything he could to help me from that point onward. His office hours are incredibly chill and helpful, and I encourage anyone struggling in his course to attend them as much as possible. He truly wants everybody to do well in his course and that is clearly reflected in his lessons, often asking for feedback and tweaking his lessons to fit people's preferences. Also one of the funniest teachers I have ever had, and he seems to really enjoy teaching. Please take him if doing well is your goal.

This guy is the most awesome TA and I would highly recommend taking his section if given the chance. He answers every question you ask him in a very educating way and he possesses that certain curiosity of the world that you will only encounter once or twice in your life.

He's not the worst professor, and a lot of the reviews below are probably a little harsh. Early in the semester it was a little rough, with him leaning into theory on the harder side, but he began using more example problems to clear up concept confusion. He gave homeworks that were definitely tough, but began to give lots of bonus point questions on them. He also curved every exam to an 83 average. I think he can definitely improve on his teaching, but it is definitely possible to do well in the class if you practice concepts.

KYEONGWON LEE: Kind and understanding instructor who is able to address student concerns. There is more to be done to better this course, since it seems he is relatively new to the university, but it wasn’t bad towards the end. Things just got better. LECTURES (Rating: 4/5): Lectures are primarily based off of PowerPoint slides. This isn’t the professor’s fault but mainly that of the statistics department. It would have been more appreciated to have a curriculum where we have some practice in lectures. This eventually changed towards the end when we sent him emails. See the “Homework” section for more details about the R sessions, which were held occasionally. DISCUSSIONS (Rating: 4/5): It would’ve been nice to have two discussions for this class. We go over a practice worksheet and then head into a quiz (we leave early afterwards). The quizzes should only take 15 minutes, so it would’ve been more ideal to have the extra 5 minutes to go over worksheet problems. HOMEWORK (Rating: 2.5/5): There was only really one homework assignment for the course - an R Project that was worth 10% of our grade. The R Sessions that were intended to prepare us for this project did not help much, and it was not fun having to learn an entire programming language from scratch just for this project (I am new to R). I HIGHLY RECOMMEND TAKING DATA 110 AS A CO-REQUISITE IF YOU TAKE THIS COURSE. QUIZZES (Rating: 3.5/5): Quizzes were meh. They were given weekly in discussion and were based off of the practice problems. The class group chat panicked at first because of how unprepared the class felt for the quizzes. But eventually the averages got better over time and even I was shocked at how good I was doing. Because some quiz means were so low he plans to drop the lowest score. EXAMS (Rating: 5/5): The exams were not bad, I’m just dumb. (I also have neither the dorm nor the time to study.) Dr. Lee allows you to bring a formula sheet in for the exam. One side of a sheet for the midterm, and the whole sheet for the final. Oh, and did I forget to mention there’s extra credit? OVERALL RATING: 3.8/5 Structure for Fall 2025 - R Project (10%) - Quizzes (30%; weekly, lowest dropped - we had nine) - Midterm Exam (25%) - Final Exam (35%)

Teaching & Materials: He is a good professor in terms of giving the content clearly and having a lot of recordings, slides, and practice to look at during the lectures and discussions. However, he was a bit monotone so every lecture I attended kind of went in one ear and out the other. Content Difficulty & Background: The content really was not that bad at all, but I didn’t take CSA in high school so I think seeing this for the first time might be the reason why a lot of people do poorly. Exams: The exams throughout the semester were fair for me, but I thought the final was much more difficult than the exams we saw during the year. Study Advice: Overall, I recommend reading through slides and watching through lectures to review. Practice exams/quizzes were way easier than the actual exams, so lowkey just focus on understanding the content, syntax, and definitions more than memorizing what’s on the practice exams because those concepts probably won’t be what’s on your actual exam. Overall Experience: I am taking him for 132 too, so I had a pretty good experience!

In my opinion, Herman is a vastly underrated professor. He has three midterms and a final, and each is worth about 15-18% of your grade. He posts a 20-30 page long practice test about a week before each exam, thats filled with practice questions that are formatted and cover similar content as the corresponding exam. Basically, if you do the whole practice test and understand everything within it, you are set for the actual exam. He also posts worksheets in the form of optional homework that are good practice for exams. In terms of exam grading, he and his TA's are generally pretty generous with the grading, and I often found myself getting a higher grade than I expected. In terms of lectures, he doesnt allow electronics, which didnt really affect me as I dont use electronics in any of my classes, but he tends to be a pretty good lecturer. He covers the material at a good pace, and is very open to questions about the content. Hes also pretty funny and seems to care about his students imo. He and his TAs have plenty of office hours, and when he didnt have time to cover certain material in class, he went out of his way to make videos about it rather than direct us to the textbook to learn it ourselves, he also gave everyone three pieces of candy for halloween. He does incentivise people to come to lecture and discussion by having "surprise" graded worksheets that are cumulatively worth about 10% of the grade, so if you go to lecture and discussion, you basically get a free 10% of your grade as the worksheets are graded on completion. He also has participation points that are worth 3% of your grade where you basically have to participate a few times over the sem, so another easy 3%. As for projects, none of them were super hard, I think the longest one took me like 3 hours, he released the grades for the first two fairly quickly but waited till the end of the sem for the rest of them. He gives long instructions for the projects which have a lot of helpful details and as long as you follow that and style your code correctly you should be fine, he also gave extra credit for some of them if you finish them before the deadline. Basically, Herman is a good lecturer who cares about his students and gives ample resources and grade boosters so you can get a good grade in the class, just make sure to attend lectures and discussions and you should do fine.
Larry Herman kindled my love for systems programming. He models what a lecturer should be: engaging and clear. I see now after many years that he's one of UMD's best.

Very boring lectures and sometimes doesn't explain the reasoning behind his work. You'll going to be doing a lot of self teaching compared to other classes because sometimes he'll mention an important topic or thing you'll need to know and never mention it again and sometimes skip it if its a step he taught. What makes it better is the lecture slides sometimes have no direct lesson or topic you pull out by looking at it. Instead you will need to go to his scanned pdf file of work done in class and scroll to find your answer you were hoping to get (Or sit there and open up the panapto recording and scroll through the hour and 15 minute video). Quizzes are relatively easy and thanks to the TA for babying our class or most would've struggled. The midterms are also really not like the exam or home works. They are a step above of what he'll teach or go over in class, some of it is already tricky but I really do not feel like spending hours everyday reteaching things that I need to get taught, not what I signed up. Takeaway: Knowledgeable dude but also so boring. Teaches like you already know all of the material. Do not take Teli for 250 unless you're into self teaching yourself a lot.

This is the first time I felt like I walked away from a class with genuine real world skills, and this is exactly what Max aims for. This class is completely what you make of it. If you do the bare minimum and want a free A from an elective, avoid. If you want to become a better Data Scientist, Max's course will take you to the next level. To me, the lectures felt like YouTube videos and I walked away having learned something new after every lecture. Max is very different from lecturers we are used to. He makes his exams extremely difficult to make you truly understand concepts instead of memorizing, but they get curved and you have a lot of opportunity for extra credit to make up for them. Tips to succeed: - go above and beyond on the projects and get creative with it, Max will give you a lot of extra credit and lets you put them on your resume - do every reading Max assigns and know the core concepts of them before exams, he'll ask related questions - expect really difficult exam. use the practice exams purely to test your knowledge rather than learn from. Much of the learning for me was watching YouTube videos to better visualize the concepts. - do NOT take if you're not interested in data science, but if you are, 320 with Max will be the best class you'll take in college - Attend lectures, they're super entertaining and gives you hints on the exams

Gave good examples during class and in his notes which helped with assignments in the course, especially projects. Lectures are definitely disorganized at times with him jumping around content. But when he is focused, you are able to learn a lot in class plus he is a funny guy. Anwar or Cliff? Doesn't matter. The course is the same no matter what so just choose the lecture time that works best for your schedule.

As other reviews had stated, pretty good on the workload and the way the exams are similar, no curveballs. The projects all have bread crumbs so it's 80 percent copy and paste and 20 percent work. If anything his TAs are pretty decent and care easy to reach.

I will start this review by affirming that Justin is one of the best lecturers at all of UMD, and going to his lectures is the best way to experience the professor. On top of that, he has some of the most thorough online study material, which covers everything he lectures about, and more. He answers questions through email and piazza, and if you score poorly on an assignment, it's rarely due to ambiguity (I would say never, but his 351 exams had many poorly phrased questions that were revised mid-exam). Onto the structure of the class, this is where things become controversial. If you are in the third of UMD students that went to an MCPS high school, the class structure will be very familiar. There are seven total midterms, at least one being dropped. This means a midterm every other Friday, including the second, and last Friday of the semester. The course starts at full speed, and finishes at full speed. The entire semester is midterm season. There are numerous upsides to having this many midterms though, which other students fail to point out. Each exam is only worth 11% of the grade, and only covers two weeks of material. This puts much less weight on any individual exam, and I personally got a B on multiple exams and still finished the class with a high A. The constant studying does cause occasional burnout, but it also prevents the midterm season cramming that many students tend to do, and prevents you from falling too far behind. Justin is an amazing lecturer, and the midterm schedule may sound daunting, but the condensed test material really helps prevent bad midterm habits.
