The projects aren't that bad, as long as you sit down and do them with a couple days of time to work since they can involve a lot of writing code even if its straightforward. My only issue with the projects is the same issue I have with quizzes and assume I will have with the exams: the requirements (or on assessments the phrasing of questions) is usually so poor that they simply don't make sense or are missing key details for you to do the work. It's been the case on every project so far that there is an absolute deluge of posts asking "what does this actually mean" about project specs, because the phrasing of a spec will be vague enough that you could interpret it many different ways and the public tests will be so incredibly simple that they don't address a single one of the clarifications needed. There's also often not actually any details given on expected formatting for things that require formatting, and TAs/instructor will sometimes give conflicting answers with each other to questions. Whether I end this class with a C- or an A+ I'll leave having learned the exact same amount from the lectures and projects: absolutely nothing. The fact UMD is ranked as high as it is for CS and then has professors for lower level classes that cannot teach and TAs which vary from "make the class easy as pie" to "Lecture round 2 with no benefit to the students at all" is rather insane. You would think it in the school's interest to attempt to give students a strong foundation so they can confidently get internships, do research, do well in later classes, but I'm pretty sure the avg student coming out of this class will only have gained the knowledge that "they don't like C/assembly" based on a bad prof.

CMSC250 is meant to be your introduction to proofs and mathematical rigor in Computer Science and I did not get that at all from this class. Lecture was relatively easy to follow and he was an engaging lecturer. However, he hand-waved a lot of things that I felt shouldn't have been handwaved. For example, we never really did structural induction like Fawzi's class did, instead he just kind of gave an outline of what it would look like. He is also a bit disorganized and him and his TAs were all five minutes late to one of our exams. There was a proof on our first exam that was unlike anything we had done up to that point which was rather annoying. Overall his class was fine, but I would recommend taking a different professor for 250 if Maksym is one of the options. His class may be easier to get a higher grade in, but it will come back to bite you when you have to write proofs for other classes in the future.

The goat Super lenient on grading and is funny and entertaining in lecture. I really enjoyed the loose homework style with few guidelines, especially HW4 where you make a slide deck. Max continue to be silly

Cliff has a lack of professionalism that radiates throughout this entire class. He doesn’t hold his TAs to any standards so they often show up late and are unhelpful during discussions and office hours. He tries to be goofy by putting bizarre “brain rot” style questions on midterms, which obviously makes the questions way harder to comprehend. He also never responds to emails. On top of all that, he’s not a great lecturer. He’s not the Devil. I don’t want to be too harsh. But I struggle to come up with any positive contribution that Cliff made to this course that I can’t also attribute to Anwar. I would recommend taking Anwar instead.

nelson markets the class as "the easiest a you'll ever get in cs", and he isn't wrong per se. the projects are fairly straightforward (and the majority of the code for them can be found scattered across his lecture examples), although i know some students had issues with mongodb, which was in the last project so i'd definitely at least set up your projects early to troubleshoot potential issues. the exams for fall 2024 were also very similar to spring 2024, although spring 2024 was completely different from fall 2023, so take that how you will. honestly, this class is pretty chill if you're just looking for an upper level cs course, but is also very basic in what it covers (html, css, js, node, express, mongodb). nelson himself is the goat however so 5 stars

Ting is a very nice and kind prof and she really cares about her students. HOWEVER, her lectures are atrocious. She just reads of slides and writes over them with her mousepad so it is very messy. Additionally, her accent doesn't help either, so going to lecture and trying to pay attention is so hard. If you have Ting with 351 and Justin(the goat) is teaching, do yourself a favor and look at his notes and go to his lectures. I only went to tings lecture on the first day, exam review, and exam days. Moving on to exams, you will want to take her (if she is coteaching with justin) because her exams were easier than justins and more straightforward, no curveballs, and she grades leniently. Even for homework, I forgot to submit something once and she let me submit it late (whereas justin didnt let my friend submit late). Overall, she is a very nice and caring person but her lectures are not it whatsoever.

Lectures are fine but not always intitative, she often goes into depth and detail about concepts without actually introducing them or what they do. A lot of topics are realted to each other but its often unclear how. Homework and Exams are fine, exams are more conceptual while homeworks are more problem solving. This kind of thru people off midterm as she said Hw was enough study material. Not a fan off her projects, you basically completing an already implemented project. For be felt less like working with the concept we learned and more like rearrange someone elses code to make it work. Debugging was not easy as public test produce large text output which is not easy to understand.
terrible prof, terrible TAs. Refuse to make an elms page. website has wrong information. projects are very old, lecture has 0 to do with project.

Yizheng was really nice when I talked to her and willing to explain things to help; frequent pauses were made at lecture to ask for questions, and there were always a few active students who were engaged and had interesting conversations. A LOT of the class did not attend regularly (probably in part because the exams mostly graded on slides) but there were good explanations of how the relevant architecture and network protocols led to vulns and i think everyone who actually went to class did well in it. Abt the negative reviews below, I think the projects were relatively straightforward with a good autograder for the parts that were autogradeable. I think that there was some annoyance by people about slow grading of some free response questions on the projects, but I think you could tell pretty easily what you'd get on the project because you'd know pretty obviously if your exploit went off well. The grade distribution of the class was better than for other sections, and followed a similar grading schedule, so while I think that some of the content was difficult it surely wasn't as bad as some people are making it out to be

Exhausting semester. I get why he did so many exams. I get it let me study fewer topics per exam. I probably did better because of it. But it was non-stop like no class since first year has been for me.

So this is my second semester in a row taking Max, after I had him last semester too in CMSC320. Meaning, I am pretty confident in all of the things that follow. Just trust me—don't take him if you don't have to. He is very disorganized, has terrible exam questions, decent projects, awful slides and lectures, bad TAs. At least he is a nice guy.

never in my life have I took a worse class than this, you learn nothing, homeworks are useless, projects are useless, class is useless. You go to lecture get confused, leave lecture, try to self study, cant even do that because the textbook is bad, do homework (its very easy), do projects (its very easy), then you feel confident and walk into the exam and leave knowing that you have in fact learnt nothing and everything was a waste of time.

cons - lectures are boring and a little bit disorganized - chooses the wildest colors for his slideshows(one had teal blue background with red or pink text) - very memorization focused - I don't think I really learned that much - english is not his first language so we spent a lot of time debating over the wording of homework questions and the TAs were pretty rude and unhelpful when asked for clarification(everyone I knew was confused) pros - easy - not that much work structure of the class: biweeky quizzes(fairly easy), 1 midterm, final exam(fairly straightforward). He gives mostly similar practice questions weekly homeworks - mostly fill in the blank vocabulary type things which were easy(if you understood what was being asked which was not given), a couple coding homeworks which were a lot harder

He's good. Knows what he's talking about, very approachable, and genuinely wants to see students succeed. He might not come off this way though if he doesn't think you're truly interested or even paying attention, but I think that's fair. Sometimes his organization does confuse me, especially so in this class where I already a little confused to start (low level coding is my weakness). Oh, and also, he's funny. For the class, please start projects early and try to understand the concepts because it's very satisfying. I would say this class is hard, but I know a lot of people would think it's easy.

An excellent professor. He is very helpful and informative during office hours and he answers questions very quickly on Discord. He is very understanding and will sometimes give students additional time to complete assignments and also does a great job of explaining important concepts in class.

Overall, this is an amazing class and you learn so much. It's definitely hard but definitely worthwhile to take if you're interested in designing algorithms. Mount is the absolute GOAT too. He's an incredible teacher and you can get a lot of help on the HW by simply running your approach by him. Midterm average was around a 78, but he curves at the end of the course. He also records! The only gripe I have with the course is that there are only 5 HW's, which makes each HW every time consuming and stressful. I would've preferred more HW's with less problems per HW to spread out the workload. However, I still really loved this course. It was so satisfying when I finally got a working algorithm, and I feel like I got so much better at it.

This class is flipped lecture which means we watch the lecture videos on our own, and go into class to ask questions for one of the classes for the week. The other class for the week (not listed on testudo as a class/discussion time) is a workshop where we do an assignment on that week's lecture content. The content of the course is ok. It's all pertinent to the subject, and is realistic for students to learn at this level. However, the logistics for this class and it's assignments were some of the worst I've ever taken at CS at Maryland. This professor does not teach, and it feels like he does not care about this class at all. He was not present at the midterm to answer questions, and when we asked the TA's questions at the midterm, they said "Let me ask the Professor" and then the professor would not respond, so the TA's did their best in answering our questions for the midterm. Every homework assignment released with bugs, meaning if you wanted to start the homework early, you'd have to post on piazza about the bug, wait for the TA's to fix it, and then start again. Every homework assignment had extremally vague instructions and grading criteria spawning many questions on the piazza. These questions were often answered by complete non answers, or "you should know this". Might I add that the in person question sessions were not recorded, so if you could not remember what a TA/Professor said during class, there was no way to get that answer. So, if they answered a piazza question in class, you're just left hoping another student will answer it for you. In completing the homeworks, many of the lecture videos were wholly unhelpful as well. The videos are not substantial enough to teach the content to a level needed to complete the homeworks in my opinion. To complete them, I would go back to reference the lecture videos, only to realize he spent maybe a sentence or two on implementation details we need for the homework, and the rest of the video introing why this technique is important in history, or why it fell out of favor. All in all, the class felt lazy, sloppy, and an absolute nuisance to complete assignments. I strongly recommend against taking CMSC470 with this professor.

We'll get it out of the way: he's a great guy, tries to remember everyone's name, and definitely wants people to learn. He also had a monologue at the end of class about using coding to do good in the world which I thought was very sweet. The class utilizes a flipped classroom format: you have to watch a series of videos about the subject of the week, do a small assignment due before class, then a small group assignment on Monday, Wednesday goes over content and Friday is supposed to introduce most stuff for the week. I don't dislike this format inherently, but a lot of the lectures are just repetitions of the content. Sometimes it dipped into genuinely neat material, but most of the time I walked away from class thinking "why did I come here?" My only answer was for the participation credits, which is never great. Exams feel a bit at cheap at times, but with four non-cumulative exams they aren't the worst thing in the world. Homeworks hold your hand a bit too much, the group project has some very strange requirements about using very specific techniques. Our group assignment was to make a game, but the scope of what a game was defined as was extremely nebulous. Besides the group project, I didn't really feel like any assignment took up an unfair amount of time, especially given that this is the MAIN programming course for InfoSci. It could've afforded to go a little further and more in-depth, but the flipped classroom format gives you the skills to look things up. Also, the comments about grades taking forever to come in is true. It's not fun not knowing where your standing is in the class, and I was almost certain of where I was. Group project felt really rushed, we straight up had multiple assignments get auto-100%'d because of how far behind on grading he was. Very excited about the material, and I still would recommend him, but he could stand to use time better in lecture/on the schedule in general, and generally have a more organized class.

Absolutely terrible experience. Hannah, the TA, was consistently rude and dismissive—interrupting students mid-sentence and making it feel like asking questions was a burden. She clearly shouldn’t be in a teaching role. As for Professor Duffy, she seemed completely checked out. Grading took forever, and she even told us not to reach out to her directly—everything had to go through Hannah first, which only made things worse. The whole setup felt disorganized and honestly disrespectful to students. It seemed like they were more interested in power-tripping than actually helping us learn.

This was my favorite class of the semester. The professor is always kind, helpful, and creates a good environment in the classroom. His explanations can be convoluted at times, but the professor is always open to questions and makes an effort to reiterate difficult topics. I appreciate how he keeps assignment expectations clear and wants his students to succeed in the course.

Her pre-recorded video lectures are very helpful. I feel like I have learned a lot from her class so far. Labs, quizzes, and programming assignments are reasonable. I have never felt like there are concept she hasn't explained that are needed on the assignments, but YMMV. Exams have also been fair. Grading does take a while which is quite irritating, although I feel like this is how most of my classes are. She provides her powerpoints which is very helpful for quizzes and exams. Did I mention everything is open note? It's wonderful.

You need a really good TA and previous calc knowledge if you want to pass this class. The material is actually light but because the professor is so buns, everyone basically got horrible grades for the exams, especially the first one. Don't even bother with the textbook either, it's a lot of unnecessary information just to explain a simple concept and the problems the professor chooses for the syllabus are not great either. Do the practice exams and watch Organic Chemistry Tutor videos and you'll be set, just don't go to her lectures
He gets a bad rep but overall a very good guy. Just go to office hours atleast once a week and do your suggested problems. everything else falls into place.

The absolute goat TA and the only reason I was able to do somewhat decent in the class. I wasn't able to attend many lectures due to various reasons throughout the entire semester. However, Qi'an ensured that I never lagged behind. He explains every single topic explained in lecture again and gives proper examples and questions to solve. He write all his notes and comes to class super well prepared and answered every question we had. Before exams, whenever professor Wong uploaded practice questions, Qi'an on his own used to upload answers to all those questions and used to post any additional theory questions that could help us. He was an amazing TA and always tried his best to help us and was really understanding. He's the GOAT.

I'm writing this review just after the final exam for Stat 400. It being his first time teaching at the university, Zheng started the year off rough, with confusing lectures, he was initially bad at explaining topics and gave no insight into what was going to be on each exam. After students expressed their complaints, he really cleaned up his act. For exam #2, he told us what type of problems would be on the exam and gave out practice problems similar to ones on the exam. He also began to give out extra credit points on the homework, which made it easier to recover points. For the final, we were allowed a double sided a4 sheet of notes, and he gave us in-depth practice problems that were very relevant to the problems on the final. I'm giving him a 4 star review because he really turned his teaching style around and doesn't deserve many of the 1 star reviews he was given by students early in the semester, when he was still acclimating to being a teacher for the first time. He also responds quickly to emails and is generally a pretty funny guy in lecture. Please don't shy away from taking his class because of the people who gave him low ratings early in the semester who were upset by their exam 1 results.

I'm not sure what's going on in this class anymore. The STAT department needs to do something about its courses and professors. First there's the nightmare with Dr. Zheng's STAT400 class and Dr. Williams teaching STAT410 in the most brutal way, then there's this. Dr. Lee does not seem to go over the concepts effectively at all, instead redirecting us to his practice worksheets whose answers are typically not gone over. This makes doing them a waste of time as we can't even check our solutions to see where we went wrong. The quizzes in this class also have abysmal averages (two quizzes didn't even get a PASSING mean, with one being under 50%). This shows how unprepared many of us feel, even though the quizzes were pulled directly from the practice worksheets. The funny part? ALMOST NOTHING from the lectures shows up in the worksheets, lecture is all PowerPoint slides with conceptual stuff but the discussion is entirely applications of these concepts, which wasn't taught very well. The professor also seems to be very static with learning and doesn't seem to change things up very well. Our midterm review was literally just the professor going back through the very first set of slides and jumping through things, rather than doing practice problems that would be useful for the exam. Recently, we have also had a sub instructor cover the class, and the sub literally went BACK TO THE START of a 90-ish slide PowerPoint that we were MIDWAY through, jumping through slides very quickly. The class GroupMe had also freaked out several times when there were quizzes because everyone felt so unprepared. I hope there's a curve in this class. If so, I'll reconsider my current rating.

Pedram is a good CMSC131 Professor. The lectures are really good at explaining the concepts. As a person who never took AP Comp Sci and wasn't familiar with OOP, he did a really good job explaining it and other concepts I wasn't familiar with like recursion. His drawings of memory maps really help you understand what's going on. The other reviews are right that his lectures can be a bit monotone and on days where I was a bit tired it was easy to drift off. The projects are nice and straightforward and you shouldn't have trouble finishing them if you start on time and get help if you need it. The quizzes and exams are all doable. I know some people say he has hard exams (and it does seem to be this way compared to Elias and Nora), but they're all doable if you know the content from the lecture and do the practice he gives you. He also gives you nice review material for each quiz and exam (except for the final). Tips to succeed: - Attend every lecture. Attending them in-person helps you learn all the content at a nice pace. - Attend discussion. Before quizzes and exams, they are very useful for review and letting you know what will be on the quiz/exam. They are also helpful for learning specific things you may need for the projects and giving extra examples/questions to solidify the concepts. Some content (not a lot) is only taught in discussion. - Start projects early, try not to push them to the last minute. You’ll learn more from them. - Have a plan to study for each quiz/exam. This doesn’t have to be super thought out, but plan enough that you don’t need to cram the day before/of. A decent bit of time before each quiz or exam, Pedram will post details about it on Piazza where he usually gives a worksheet to work through and past papers. At least, give yourself enough time to work through all of it without rushing. Do all the practice he gives you. Going through the code examples in the zip files provided with each slide and making sure you understand what’s going on can be helpful. Exams and quizzes combined are a large part of the class grade so prepare for them well.

Larry Herman has a lot of quirks, and I can see why most people seem to dislike him; I, however, thought he was overall a good instructor. His lectures are well taught, and he explains concepts very well. Discussions are spent doing worksheets, which are occasionally graded for completion. He also will occasionally and randomly hand out graded worksheets during lectures--this, combined with the fact that he doesn't record lectures, means you should definitely attend as many classes as you can. His project descriptions are incredibly long and often repetitive, but this is also an advantage; you're essentially told exactly how to do each project in the description. I personally didn't find his exams to be challenging--anything he says in class or writes on the slides or handouts is fair game, and he will definitely test you on even things we spent the smallest amount of time on, but he gives a LOT of good exam prep, from the practice exams, the homeworks, and the discussion worksheets (he even admitted in lecture that he will sometimes pull exam questions from discussion worksheets, so definitely do the worksheets!). He has some negative quirks, such as not allowing electronics in class, having an interesting participation system, and being really touchy over being called a professor for some reason, but honestly the only strong negative I have for him is how incredibly long it took for everything to get graded. We had a total of 10 projects throughout this course, and by the time finals came around, we still only had the first three graded; it can be stressful, because you really don't know how well you're doing in the class if you can't know your grades until the very end. Overall: Good lecturer & exams are very passable once you understand his format, but he has a bunch of odd quirks and he's an INCREDIBLY slow grader. He's not the best instructor out there, but definitely not as bad as some of the other reviews have said. If you're forced to take his class, don't fret! Put in the work and you'll do fine. I'm giving him 4 stars because I can't give him a 3.5.

Oh Yoon, Oh Yoon, where do I start? This was single-handedly the most BEAUTIFUL class I've ever taken during my long, long, 7 years at College Park, Maryland. Yoon explains things so beautifully even a monkey could understand assembly and linux. I'm convinced the 85% of the class that gets below an A has an iq between 41 and 67. I showed my pet goldfish the Yoon lectures (he didn't record them, so I uploaded them myself using my neuralink) and he showed up to the lecture and got a 97 on the final. He invoked such an incredible passion for low-level programming in me I decided to skip the entirety of my undergrad and do a PHD at Tsinghua in compilers. I came to class every day, and he handed me extra points for simply existing, because he's such a beautiful soul. GOON WITH YOON! #YOONERS

I don't get the hate with Fawzi. I followed his conventions and copied his style for all the proofs we did and I always received good grades. He can grade harshly, one of my friends definitely experienced that, I think it just depends on whether you fully understand the subject and how to do the proof properly. As long as you stay on top of things, you'll be fine, and he makes it pretty easy to do that. It helps to write your proofs the way he demonstrates in class. I do recommend going to every lecture, he shows useful examples, explains things well, and makes the classes interesting and funny. I recommend taking him for any course that you can.

If you just want the credit, by all means, I see no reason to dissuade you. The homeworks are long, but you have plenty of time. The exams are overall pretty fair, and the group project is a fine opportunity to do research on something you're genuinely interested in. However, I cannot in good conscience recommend this professor due to the heinous amount of AI-generated material passed off as course materials. There are small slights everywhere, from the cover image of the syllabus being a blatantly AI-generated mess to convoluted, substance-lacking paragraphs hitting every AI red flag scattered throughout the supplemental material she "wrote" herself, but my least favorite of them is the class slides. There are two lecture slides that both have what are clearly screenshots of ChatGPT-generated text slapped on. One of them has black squares covering the fact that the headers start with 4.1 4.2 4.3, which implies she generated a lot more content than she showed and could have just hid it better, and using it to any extent breaks trust and brings into question all of her lecture material, but I digress. It's possible you don't have as visceral a hatred for artificial intelligence as I do, especially if you're taking a class on data science, but if you think, as I do, that lecture content in a college course that you pay money for should not be a bunch of AI-generated bullet points read back to you, I would suggest looking for another professor. Hopefully, one of your alternatives has a different stance regarding the use of AI in teaching.

Not sure if Anwar is the one who does this, but I hate the structure and organization of this class. The only practice tools are old exams and quizzes which most where in a different curriculum and language entirely. The questions on old quizzes are also significantly different than the quiz I took. There are quizzes randomly assigned Friday close to midnight and due Sunday without any warning. Everything is on only on gradescope and nothing is on elms.

Probably the easiest 300/400 level course in the CS department. If you put effort in not falling behind and starting the projects early, you will succeed. Nelson is great at explaining concepts when he’s not joking around. My one complaint is that I wish he didn’t joke around as much, but that wasn’t a big deal. I just watched the lecture recordings since you can skip around and speed up the vids. Great prof for an easy and useful class.

She’s a great person, and it’s clear that she really wants all her students to succeed, but her lecturing abilities are atrocious. If she co-teaches with Justin, you’ll be fine as long as you go over his notes or attend his lectures. If she isn’t co-teaching, I’d look for other options.

This may be the worst course I've taken at UMD. The material is artificially made 20x more confusing than it is (and it's already pretty confusing) by Dr. Yoon's disorganized, scattered lecture style. I never knew how topics were connected or how they related to each other or how they fit into the bigger picture of the course. We were given maybe 1-2 examples of problems to solve for each topic (if that), but most of the exams were problem solving variations of topics we had not seen examples for. We were similarly expected to solve homeworks entirely on our own with no peer help, when we had never seen examples of those problems before in lecture or otherwise. And this would be fine if the problems were straightforward, but he usually throws in a little curveball that completely changes the entire approach to the question. And then, on top of all that, he teases us by saying the homework problems and exam problems will seem "so simple" when we see the solutions. It was infuriating every time. You will likely pass the course if you take it, because he curves. But you will waste a whole 4xx level on material that was so poorly conveyed that you'll forget it all in a month. Avoid if you can.

I've had Shankar for CMSC 216 and CMSC 412. Although Shankar has a stutter if you focus during lectures, write down some notes, and ask him questions, he will clear up any confusions you have. The difficulty of the exams he gives usually is written by whoever is proctoring the course. In CMSC 216, the exams given were written by Yoon so it was pretty hard. In CMSC 412, Shankar wrote his own exams, which were rather fair if you knew the material (much fairer than exams written by Yoon or Kruskal). The reason why I give Shankar 4 stars is literally because I think he did an ok job teaching 412. I think reviewing a professor's competence should account for the conditions of the course. The biggest change Shankar could've done is go over hints for the projects in the lecture, though this was mostly the job of the discussion section and the TAs. Other changes Shankar could've made were to make his slides less vague and provide more detailed practice exam solutions. 412 is hard because doing the GeekOS projects take too long, leaving students without much time for other classes and to understand other aspects of Operating Systems not implemented in GeekOS. GeekOS is designed by a UMD graduate, Jeffrey Hollingsworth, Neil Spring, etc. If one accounts for the fact that this project was given to everyone who took CMSC 412, one would realize that this pain is not the fault of the Shankar but the curriculum of the course. Sure Shankar could've changed this curriculum but I don't think this would be too fair.

This class is terrible with this professor. The allure of being able to procrastinate on the assignments and projects makes you think taking this class with this professor is a good idea, but it is not. The slides are useless, going to class is useless, the videos are useless. The project descriptions are so vague and basically require you to fill in the gaps with knowledge you shouldn't be assumed to have. The projects are the hardest I've personally taken at this university - not because they were lengthy or anything, but because the content was simply not taught to us. Literally nothing is taught to us in class that can be useful for the projects. I'm actually interested in the content of the course, but it's not being taught in a way that is beneficial. This professor and this teaching style sucks and only stresses you out more. 0/5 terrible instruction please avoid and don't make the same mistake I did.

Giving him a 5 bcuz that extra exam drop came in clutch. The reason most students consider him the GOAT is because he is open to taking feedback from students which is a GOAT mindset to have as a professor.

Pratap is pretty good as a professor. He explains concepts in a coherent way, he's pretty understanding, and overall just a solid professor. Any complaints I have are directly against the organization/logistics of the class. Practice exams had some wrong answers which tripped me up, and responses on Piazza vary a LOT. Usually, it's on the much longer end. Class content itself is alright. I did learn a lot, but the content is directly taken from Berkeley's class. It's funny too; I looked up something from the slideshow for more information about that topic and all I found was the same slideshow on 4 different universities' websites. I'd recommend taking Pratap, and probably 421. Class is relatively easy too.

While he does have an accent (not really his fault) he does try to make sure you understand all of the math behind a lot of the ml algorithms. He doesn't test on the math behind the ml algorithms so that means some of the lectures are on content that isn't going to be tested but that's because he's being nice by not putting insane math on the exams. For the homework, you only have 3 so it's really not that much work overall. If you start early, you'll be fine since it takes a good amount of time to train the models. Honestly, if you go to class, take notes, and start the assignments when they come out, you'll do fine in the class and not spend much time on it. Most of the troubles with grading and such is due to incompetent TAs not him. In my opinion the review about him being incompetent is likely salty because they didn't go to class at all and started homework at the last minute.

Workload was high, but I learned a lot. If you want to take the easy version of 424, take it with Herve. But I'm glad I took it with Abadi since it covers more material and the assignments and quizzes make you learn it at a surprisingly deep level. Exams were hard only because there were no "free questions". *Every single question* required you know something a little deeper than the surface content. This was brutal for people that only had time to get a surface understanding of the material during the semester. But for me, they were fine, especially after the curve. I definitely got more questions wrong in this class (on the quizzes and homeworks) than in any other class I have ever taken, but the experience of getting some of the corner case questions wrong on the homework quizzes helped me become more sensitive of these corner cases (e.g. handling of NULLs) and I learned more as a result (and it didn't really affect my grade since the quizzes are only worth 5% of the final grade).

Milijana is a pretty solid professor, but not a super engaging lecturer. Like other reviews mention, the class is basically just David Van Horn's curriculum, so professor doesn't matter much. I stopped going to lecture about a month into the semester and just read the very good notes on the course website. Also shoutout Pierce for answering literally every Piazza question. This class will test your programming skills. Many of the assignments took me hours of debugging to figure out, especially the ones that were heavy on assembly (sidebar, the CMSC4xx info website says this class uses Ocaml, but it instead uses Racket which I found way more annoying). If you had a hard time with assembly in 216 or Ocaml in 330, this class will be a challenge. The entire curriculum is basically writing and rewriting a compiler for Racket itself, with progressively more and more features. I thought all the projects were really engaging, so I didn't mind how hard they were. The two midterms and final project, despite being take home, are pretty crazy jumps in difficulty though. Implementing runtime exception handling in assembly was a truly painful experience.

Amazing professor. Often grants extensions if he feels the class needs it, and ensures we understand the projects fully so that we are all successful. The midterm was really difficult, but projects are manageable so a good grade is definitely doable.
Does everything he can to help you, makes things interesting and there's less but larger assignments and homeworks. Has a curve on top of maximizing your scores for your grade. Amazing all around.

She's kind and it's clear that she's trying. It's also clear that she's very knowledgeable about NLP. However, that did not translate to being able to teach well. Lectures were extremely dry and often hard to follow. It was often unclear what we had to know (vs what is just "good to know"), as lectures tended to contain a lot of superfluous detail. Concept explanations were made more complicated than they had to be. On the plus side, homeworks were well-written, aided in understanding some concepts, and weren't too difficult. The midterm exam was also fair. So, it seems like the issue is not structural, but in the substance of how the material is taught. I think everyone says it pretty well for Bills as a teacher but I'll my say: Aric Bills is a really great person, he's really supportive, understanding, and fun to talk to and has a lot of humorous/fun interactions with the actual class. He is very active on support people outside of the class in my personal experience and I think everyone does appreciate his kindness and his patience. But in teaching, I think it could be improved. His current method of teaching his students is through videos that students must watch in their own time, alongside an small assignment due essentially every monday 9 am. These videos can be a bit long overall with some taking 1-2.5 hours in watch time total. You can get away with not having to watch all them but you won't always know what you want to prioritize or if you'll missing any crucial information. So in class (where attendence is kinda mandatory), its often just review of the assignment or concept already learned or work time. Another big thing for me was that grades were very very delayed. Grades weren't uploaded to canvas and so you'd have to input them by hand to canvas from gradescope if you wanted to know your grade but even then his grades on gradescope were very delayed (after spring break for some reason?). There was a point where it gotten 2 months behind and it was a bit frustrating seeing that. I think that the actual work and things you learn are important in your understanding and application of python in a data constructed concept and its obvious how much he is passionate and knowledge about coding but I think that the way things were taught and the way assignments were given could be improved upon.

If i could give her 0 stars, I would. She is by far the worst Professor I have had these past 3 years. The reviews on here are the complete opposite of what she is truly like as a Professor. Professor Ai is very knowledgeable and understanding. The class structure was pretty straightforward - an assignment every week and 2 larger projects. Gives little to no feedback on your work, draws out lectures and takes up multiple videos and hours worth of your time to explain information that could be done in minutes. She is. the most amazing teacher I had this year and the best math teacher I have ever had. The class is set up with class everyday with 2 discussions and 3 lectures. Dr Williams is a good lecture, super intelligent, and is happy to answer any questions that you have in person. However, any other communication is spotty and could easily take multiple weeks to respond to you. During the Fall 2025 semester, he changed his office hours multiple times and only let us know the morning of. Multiple people in my class compared his exams with other professor's exams and Williams' were noticeably more difficult. This course marks the worst grade I'll have ever gained during my entire 90 credits of higher education so far. I was literally teaching people within the course and still got a D. I know people that totally no-life'd the Fall 2025 semester as a whole and they have fine grades in the class. Not passing this class set me back an entire year in the degree pathway I was pursuing and I've resulted to completely changing my major. I'm surprised that basically every single professor that is offered during the Spring 2026 semester is rated higher than Williams (who was the highest rated available professor when I registered for the Fall 2025 semester).

Teaching & Content: Overall, he was a good professor in terms of teaching the content and giving examples of the problems we would be likely to see on tests during class. Exams: The exams were similar to the problems we covered in discussion, other than the true and false questions which were very annoying and it was easy to lose points on those. This guy really likes math. I mean really likes math. He goes on lots of tangents and tends to conceptualize things in a way that only makes sense if you read the textbook or if you're very tapped into math. Besides the fact that his teaching ability is below average, he does actually care about his students. He curves when necessary and gives you homeworks that are free points along with bonus points that you can go for to save your grade. If you actually study, you can succeed in this class but it is hard to learn from this guy. The only reason he gets 3 stars is because his fits are pretty fire.

Great professor, does not deserve his rating, had great slides and taught extremely well. As long as you do your HW and complete practice, you will be beyond fine for this class. Taught me better stat than any other professor I have had. Take him, do not believe the bad ratings.
One of the most understanding, knowledgeable, personable, and funny people I've ever met within the professional sphere of computer science. This dude is great, and buy his game on Steam.

I think people are too harsh on Herman; his average here is a 3.14, which isn't terrible, but the way I've heard older CS students speak about him is as if he is the teacher of doom and despair. (Note that I called him teacher DO NOT call him professor this will be the first thing he says on the first day and he may even spend 10 minutes giving a whole presentation on it later in the sem!) The project descriptions are quite lengthy, but personally I would prefer this to vague descriptions where you have to figure it out yourself. There will be pretty much no questions left unanswered. Some projects are quite difficult, but honestly some of the ones I struggled with the most were also the ones I left until the last day or two, so I would recommend starting around three to four days before the due date. Also, make sure you read through the whole project description before starting, I know it's annoying but it's better than if you start to code and then realize you're violating project requirements, because sometimes you are prohibited from doing things that may be intuitive. Overall though, some projects were hard, some were easy, and also bombing one or two projects is really not detrimental to your grade. He also has some nice extra credit for a lot of them if you do it early and only submit once which is super nice. As for exams, I genuinely think his exams were extremely fair. Herman gives super long practice exams that I usually found to be harder than the actual exam, if not about the same. To study I typically reviewed his slideshows, which he posts, and then did those practice exams and I did pretty well on all the exams. Even questions I got wrong on exams, I felt like they were fair questions to have been asked and things I should have known. One interesting policy to take note of, though, is the grading of multiple choice questions. These were usually the harder part of the exams. They are multi-select and you get 1 point off for selecting an incorrect answer and 2 points off for not selecting a correct answer. This is super important because if you are truly unsure, you should just select an answer because you lose less points if that's wrong than if you don't pick it and it's correct. The lectures themselves can be pretty boring, but I do think they are super helpful. In hindsight, my worst project grade was definitely as a result of me zoning out in class when going over that topic. If you listen in class, you will be pretty set because he does explain concepts well and often uses people in the front row as examples, which helps get the point across. Also, he does like to make jokes sometimes during lectures and personally I really enjoy his humor. The lectures are not necessarily mandatory, but there are graded worksheets that pop up both during lectures and mostly during discussions which are about 10% of your grade, so you really should go. Also, those worksheets are super helpful to understand what exams are like. As for homework, I'm ngl I did like 3 of them and there were probably around 10-12 not quite sure. The ones I did were helpful but they're all optional and really can just be used as additional studying. Finally, just some interesting policies that Herman has. No phones, laptops, iPads, etc. If using technology is important to you definitely don't take Herman because he is very serious about it and will call you out every single time. Don't sit in the back row because he will tell you to move up. The damn pdf password really got me it's really annoying to have a locked pdf but also thats not really that deep. There is a participation grade for 3% and he is more likely to call on you if you sit in the front (not really that crazy but good to know). He doesn't do Canvas announcements but instead has a newsfeed that won't notify you when he posts and instead you have to remember to check (this really pissed me off but also not that deep, not sure why he does this). You also can't email him or message him because he won't answer, you have to go to office hours to ask any questions and such. Finally, he has very specific style requirements. Most of them were pretty intuitive to me, the only one that sucked was that you aren't allowed to have multiple return statements, that was always so annoying but I got used to it. Overall though, I thought Herman was a very good teacher and I can honestly say I learned so much this semester. Coming from AP Comp Sci A in high school I think it's super important to have a good teacher in 132 for these foundational concepts. I know a lot of people where 132 was more review for them, but for me it was all new and I feel like I learned it very well. I recommend Herman for 132!
Super nice professor but I'm not sure if I really learned anything because his exams were practice test simulators. Projects aren't too bad tho! He's also very entertaining to watch.

i literally loved his class, but thats coming from someone who just loves riddles tbh, because i know our final hurt hella people who didnt know what was happening since everything was so vague also he does not curve or drop at ALL so expect your grade to be your grade imma be honest i took a makeup once and our TA didnt even show up til 1.5hours later which was kinda annoying but honestly its very passable

Max has roughly 20 years of experience as a data scientist prior to teaching and everything he does in class (exams, homework) is geared toward preparing someone to work in the industry, which is something I really appreciate. I think the reviewer who said "Overall a great change of pace from the rest of the CS meatgrinder classes and highly recommend" was very accurate. I'd highly recommend taking 320 with Max for this reason. (I can see why something like 250 or 351 might be awkward with him, though, since that's not his passion.) Exams are somewhat difficult but are not a huge portion of your grade individually. Homeworks are designed to mimic real-world data science assignments and are decent resume fodder, and in terms of grading, are easy 100s to boost your grade. Extra credit is also available for homeworks if you put in extra effort. As many other reviewers mention, he is disorganized, but I still found his lectures to be entertaining and educational. I would recommend attending his lectures as he deviates from his slides a lot.

I highly recommend Asgari. She's new to teaching at UMD and yet has done a fantastic job at teaching the course. PROS: - Very funny and engaging professor, I was rarely bored during lecture and actually liked going. - Homework assignments make up a great portion of the grade, making it easier to pass even if you slip up on an exam. - HW assignments are very interesting despite being vague. He might ask something like "here's a dataset, write me a report about the data," and it's up to the student to decide what to do from there. A lot of extra credit is given for creativity, effort, and generally impressing the grader, which helps boost your grade at the end of the semester. - Exam questions could pop up in data science interviews. They also force you to be well-prepared and understand the content. - Homeworks can be decent projects to put on your resume - Max is a pretty reasonable professor and is willing to help out, as long as you talk to him well ahead of deadlines. - Sometimes cancels class spontaneously, but this could also be perceived as a con since the class might fall off schedule - He gives LOTS of extra credit opportunities. I would say to do all of them; you might end up needing it at the end of the semester. Lots of it doesn't even take that long, it just involves you submitting notes for a lecture or taking a photo of you studying for an exam with a friend. CONS: - While he can be really unserious, some people might not like that style, since it can lead to distraction or falling off schedule - Exams are pretty hard and can sometimes be very poorly worded. Class averages for the first two midterms were not great (Exam 1 was roughly 66%, Exam 2 was 70%) - He can be pretty disorganized. Either he forgets to cover something in class, or just doesn't cover it at all since he spent too much time in class going on random tangents. - He takes pretty long to respond to emails. - You will need to do a lot of self teaching. He covers a little bit of pandas, but aside from that, not much code is covered at all. I had to teach myself how to use more pandas functions, Scikit-learn, and other important frameworks necessary for class. Other notes/takeaways: - Watch the 3Blue1Brown playlist on neural networks when you get to that part of the class, those were really helpful in understanding the concepts. Those concepts are also testable. - Start homework early to avoid late submission or cheating. - Do all the extra credit opportunities, they really don't take that long to do and could really help you out. Overall, he's a decent professor and I enjoyed taking the class with him.

He's not that great of a lecturer, but he's my favorite professor. He's just the best, but not the best at teaching. He's funny too :). Class in general is easy, the projects take a little while, so I'd to starting at least 2 days before the due date. I don't really understand all the hype around Nelson; he comes across as a condescending teacher. For 335, the first midterm felt like a chore, requiring you to memorize a bunch of random information. The only effective way to prepare was by studying previous midterms. For fall 2024, our midterms were nearly identical to those from the previous spring, but they’re always subject to change—spring 2024's midterm, for example, wasn’t like fall 2023's. Our semester got lucky with similar midterms, but overall, you don’t learn much in this class. I was in the 8 AM section, and while I didn’t mind the early timing, Nelson's lectures were quite boring. He often makes jokes and gets off-topic, which isn’t what I want to deal with at 8 AM. It feels like he doesn’t fully understand the material he's teaching. When asked for specifics, he often can’t provide clear answers. If something in his code doesn’t work, he doesn’t seem to know why. I already knew the basics of HTML and CSS but wanted to learn more about JavaScript and MongoDB. Unfortunately, I was disappointed—Nelson simply gave us the code for those topics without explaining how the systems work. The final exam was super easy and almost identical to Project 5. You could literally reword that project and still get full points on the final. The TAs are often PhD or master’s students, and they’re difficult to work with. They don’t provide helpful answers most of the time. This class is definitely worth taking if you’re in it for the grade, but it has its downsides. For example, the midterms aren’t given during class; instead, they’re held at 6:30 PM in a different lecture hall. While I understand Nelson’s intent to prevent one section from sharing answers with another, this setup is inconvenient. I would much prefer taking the midterms during class. Overall, I think 335 needs to be restructured. It feels outdated and poorly designed. We had to learn things from JavaScript ES5, which is deprecated—why bother teaching it? I wish they’d reduce the focus on CSS and introduce more relevant topics, like React, into the projects. A more modern framework would make this course much more worthwhile.

As I am writing this, Justin's average rating on Planet Terp is a 4.69, which is even higher than Christopher Kauffman's average rating (4.63). I had Kauffman for CMSC216 in Spring 2025, and he was one of my favorite professors of all time. Needless to say, given all the hype around Justin, I had high hopes going into his Summer 2025 CMSC351 class. Now that everything's over, I can say in short that I am disappointed with my experience. To be clear, Algorithms as a Computer Science class is commonly agreed to be a terrible class pretty much everywhere (based on talking to many people from many different universities). A large part of this is due to the fact that those with minimal experience in algorithmic programming find the class extremely difficult, while at the same time those with a lot of experience in algorithmic programming (i.e. competitive programmers, like myself) often dislike how it is taught very mathematically rigorously yet with little intuition or application at all (in other words, this class will not get you through a coding interview). Yes, Algorithms, the Computer Science class, is more of a math class than anything else. Yes, Computer Science is not just programming, and Theoretical Computer Science consists almost entirely of pure math. All of this I knew going in. None of this prepared me for when I lost over half the points on a problem from Homework 1 asking me to prove the Big Omega of a certain function. I approached it as almost everyone intuitively would; like almost everyone had been taught to solve an inequality since middle and high school. Set up the inequality. Turn it into an equality, and solve the equality. Determine which side of the solution to the equality contains the solutions to the inequality, and turn the solution to the equality back into an inequality. Apparently, this wasn't rigorous enough for this class. Perhaps this is just how this kind of stuff works. But we were never told that solving it this way would lose us points, and the "correct" way shown in lecture seemed unnecessary and unintuitive. Instead, Justin complained that many submitted solutions to such Big-Omega or Big-O proof problems looked the way AI would solve them, and that such proofs "were generally terrible", citing several reasons why. Okay, fine. If you take Justin, make sure you explain the hell out of any answer you give to a problem. One problem on Exam 1 asked me to find a lower bound for something and to show my work. I later received minimal points for my answer, despite the fact that the work I had shown lined up almost exactly with a potential full-score answer as described in the rubric. Upon submitting a regrade request, I was told the grader had no idea what I did here at all, since I had no explanation at all. But the question never asked me to explain! Too bad. There was an Exam 1 MCQ problem which asked whether a certain algorithm was O(N^2) in the best case. The algorithm in question was O(N) in the best case and O(N^2) in the worst case. As such, most people in the class answered incorrectly, as technically an algorithm which is O(N) is also O(N^2). A big stink was made on Piazza about this being a trick question hidden in a sea of 50 multiple-choice questions, designed to make students lose points even if they understood the concepts it was supposed to be testing. One student asked, to avoid confusion, why didn't Justin instead ask if the algorithm was O(N^100) in the best case? Another student literally included a screenshot of the Merriam-Webster entry for "trick question" in their post. In the end, Justin's response was that technically the algorithm was indeed O(N^2) in the best case, and that he didn't expect his students to autopilot any questions in his class. On top of this, there was a question on the Exam 2 MCQ which, depending on your interpretation of the question (the wording was not specific enough), could have had two different answers. However, if you picked the wrong one, you had no recourse, not even through Piazza. By this point, people had long since stopped posting on Piazza about questions like this. They knew nothing would result from their efforts. On Exam 3, there was a free-response question which essentially asked us to find the shortest path between two points in "a simple, connected graph" (I'm simplifying greatly). Many test takers realized quickly the looseness of this wording and realized that, to cover all graphs which could potentially be described as "a simple connected graph", one needed to run Floyd's Algorithm, as a simple BFS would not cover the case of a weighted graph, and Dijkstra's would not cover the case of negative-weight edges. Once Exam 3 was graded, everyone who wrote such a solution to that problem lost points (there was a special "tier" in the Gradescope "rubric" for Floyd/Dijkstra solutions). I asked in my regrade request what the issue with my answer was. The response was that I needed to specify what my input to Floyd's Algorithm was or what graph I was going to run it on. I responded that in my answer I had specified running Floyd's algorithm on precisely the graph described in the problem statement. The response? "It does not define distances". Confused and a little frustrated, I wandered over to take a look at the official Exam 3 solutions. The official solution to that problem? Run a BFS. Justin is not the worst professor I've ever had (currently, that (dis)honor goes to Manoussos Grillakis). Justin is not the devil. Justin is not someone who you need to avoid at all costs. But as a student in his Summer 2025 CMSC351 class, I felt like the environment I was in was just a little bit more hostile than I was used to. Every time I made a Piazza post, I was just a little bit nervous that I'd get flamed by Justin in his response. I felt a severe lack of benefit of the doubt, almost to the point of actively trying to take away points from correct or mostly correct answers. Look. Everyone's different, and everyone is looking for different things in the professors they get. Lord knows I have some unpopular opinions regarding some UMD professors (both positively and negatively). You might enjoy Justin when you take him, or he might even have just been going through something this summer. All I'm saying is, if you do decide to take him (and, to be honest, given that the alternative is Kruskal, you might decide to take him anyway): don't say I didn't warn you.

In fact she was probably the most helpful and responsive professor I had in all four years of my college experience. With that said, her lecturing can be on the weaker side but she makes up for it by again being very helpful, having excellent slides, and an abundance of practice questions. Overall would definitely recommend taking this class with Dr. Asgari.

While I took this course during the Covid Times, this Professor was an absolute Godsend. His only requirement to be able to turn in projects late was that you talk to him in his office, which was always a pleasure. He understood the particular pressure that students in his course were under, and worked with everyone who asked on a modified submission schedule. I had never had that with a single CS professor before, and it felt as the Prof. Agrawala truly wanted students to learn. As far as actually teaching went, he was very knowledgeable about the material, and had first hand experience with the making of modern operating systems, which he shared with the class. His slides are yes from the text book, but they are always available on the class website, and line up exactly with the textbook, which he provided as a free PDF (I wish all teachers did this). As long as you read the book and practice any sort of problem that he does step-by-step with the class, as well as study the project slides, you have what you need to know for the exams. He doesn't list out topics for studying, but he also prefaces his course with advice such as, "get one last good nights rest tonight, that's it for the semester," and "everything you heard about this course is absolutely true." Regardless of if it is the case, it's imperative that you get stared on the projects early, and read the textbook. This is not an easy course, and this Professor understands that, but the difficulty in the course does not stem from administrative BS or weird rules. It's hard because Operating Systems are hard, and that's the point.

The hate in here is not deserved, I do agree her class was more difficult than it should've been, but if you spoke with her she was especially kind and willing to help. It was clear to me she was definitely putting in the effort to be a better teacher.

I am writing this in response to some of the other students' reviews for CMSC420 for the fall 2025 semester. I do not want to invalidate any of their struggles or experiences. However, based on a Piazza discussion forum about the class structure that was created at the end of the semester, there were also many students who preferred the biweekly exam structure over the traditional course format whose perspectives are not currently represented. As one of these students, I found that having biweekly exams was much less stressful than having to study lots of content for a few big midterms, since each of the exams only had a few topics. The week before each exam, Justin posted a list of recommended homework problems with answer keys that would be very similar or essentially the same as the exam questions. After doing these problems each week and checking my mistakes, I felt that I understood the content well and was confident in my ability to do well on the exams. The lowest two exam grades were also dropped. Regarding Justin's perspectives on cheating, I only remembered him talking about this a few times at the beginning of the semester when he explained his rationale for the new exam structure. From then on, I don't remember him mentioning it, and all of the lectures were completely focused on the content. Throughout the semester, Justin was also very responsive to students' questions and concerns.

By far the best option you have for CMSC421 (though imperfect) Pratap is quite a nice lecturer. When looking at the slides at first (which, as AI is, is still stolen from Berkeley), some equations and concepts are kind of hard to grasp at first glance. But Pratap explains it in a simplified way while not removing the details fully. Although some of the AI concepts at the start are repetitive (BFS, DFS, and other stuff you learned), there's just enough to make the start somewhat different. Pratap records all his lectures (which lowers attendance drastically, but near the end of the semester, some lectures stopped being recorded for some reason. There were intended to be more assignments, but likely to disorganization, there were only 4 homework assignments and 1 lab. I really was hoping to do more coding (and the coding assignment was pretty easy, though these 5 assignments ended up being weighted up 10% each, crazy given the homework was also short). This may have happened due to disorganization, and really, disorganization is the main gripe I have with this class. TAs don't answer on Piazza, and Pratap answers nearly every question (I feel bad for him qwq). Homework grades come quite late, regrades are annoying, and questions are written strangely quite often. I feel that if this class were managed much better, it would be perfect, and strangely enough, more homework. Tests are easy. Like, really easy. The practice exam is extremely similar to the actual exam, so similar that it incentivizes overfitting on the practice exam (and, plus, you even have a cheatsheet for each test!). The averages were extremely high (87ish?) for each test, so that will not be a concern unless something changes. Overall, given the teachers I've seen teaching AI, be glad you have Pratap (though he's going on sabbatical...). Despite some flaws, he runs a good course for a notoriously poorly run class.

I got so discouraged by the class and how she taught things, I ended up skipping lectures, trying to watch her lectures online, getting confused, looking it up and finally getting an inkling of understanding, then getting smacked in the face with the exams. TAs sucked, grading sucked, the homework assignments sucked, and the slides sucked. If you value your time, your sanity, and your ability to exist on this mortal plane, you'll steer FAR from this professor.

I think a LOT of the reviews below saw his high reviews before last semester (that have gone down since) and thought this would be an easier class to skate through. Prof Abadi is incredibly knowledgeable about databases and it shows. This guy wants his students to learn, and if you want to do well in this class, you will have to. The biggest qualm I have with this class is that the textbook can be confusing/quite boring at times. As an extension of this, the reading quizzes based on them can get a little challenging, especially as you cover DBMS internals towards the 2nd half of the semester (though these are a pretty small part of your end grade). However, from my experience, his lectures/slides covering the info again really ironed out everything for my understanding. You will have to come to class to answer clicker questions, but most are simple and he usually gives credit for most wrong answers. Even if you picked an answer that received no credit, you could defend your thought process and he'd usually be nice enough to mark it correct anyway. Projects 3 and 4 are not trivial by any means, but I didn't find them devastatingly hard. The midterm was a bit challenging, but nothing compared to the final. You will have to study your butt off for the final, but if you can put in the time to really understand everything (mostly B trees and the DBMS algos), it's very doable. And that learning will most likely stick. Overall, I think this class is dragged the most down by the admittedly boring textbook. Maybe changing reading quizzes to be due after you learn the content in the lecture would be beneficial for this, but I'm not really sure. That all being said, if you read textbooks well and strive to truly learn in your classes, I don't think you'll regret taking this. You will have to work hard, but if you are used to doing that to excel in your other classes I wouldn't view this as some insane challenge. It's definitely been the most valuable topic I've learned, maybe just behind OS.

Amazing professor and really great class to take. She was teaching for the first time and using David van Horn's curriculum, which is generally quite good. Projects are fair and the head TA, Pierce, is ruthless in a good way. There are secret tests, thankfully, so we actually have to think about our code, proofread, and test. You are writing a compiler to x86-64 assembly, which means you don't really get helpful error messages, especially in the second half of the semester. So you have to walk through everything to make sure it's good which really builds patience and computer science skills. I was screwed over by the second midterm so badly I might not end up with an A despite getting perfect scores on everything up to that point. I trust that they'll refine the assignments so that the difficulty is not so jarring. But by itself the exams are very fair. There are 2, 24-hour (midterm) exams and 3-week final exam. I personally think the first 2 weeks were too easy but this might have been based on David van Horn's curriculum and she still had very effective lectures for people who needed the Assembly review. She goes over Racket (which she shouldn't for a 400-level class, you should just pick up on it from writing code and from the notes) and has an entire project dedicated to writing Racket. Hopefully this is refined but the second half being insanely hard really makes up for the first half being insanely easy and it cancels out.
Class itself is straightforward, but exams had tricky questions (even though they were open note and open computer)

Not only are the algorithms taught (somewhat) applicable to interviews and the job setting, but I left the semester with a much better foundation of how to think about solving algorithmic problems. I would 100% take any class this professor teaches.

Extremely boring class. Lectures are drawn out with unnecessary detail that isn't interesting either. Homeworks are laughably easy for how much they're worth, so this class is an easy A. If she's still doing video recordings in the future I recommend skipping class and reading the slides, as you're just saving yourself the time for the same grade in the end.

Uses an autograder to provide near instant-feedback, which would be fine but 1. Words cannot describe the annoyance and anger I feel towards her. The professor is knowledgable but expects us to do grad work. Please don't take the class.

She makes the subject matter really straight forward. Lectures are very clear, and she always posts class notes. Her exams are also fairly easy. The only issue I ever had with her was that it took her a VERY long time to grade exams.

I was scared going into Calc 2 as everyone said it was a weed out class but Professor Song was great. Exams were similar to problems solved done in class and she would tell us what would be on the weekly quizzes. Id say a better option for Calc 2

If you're taking linear algebra(especially as a freshman), I highly reccomend that you DO NOT take this professor. terrible, just terrible, final hit harder than a truck. his final comparatively was harder than any past finals given, he made us think it was going to be way easier. I had 98 on first mid term and a 80 on second one and I'm still probably going to fail. just think abt that.

Dr. Khurana is a wonderful professor. Her selection of topics for the class is thorough and encompasses what I hoped to learn in a Statistics 2 class. She provides notes for every topic that are detailed, organized, and easy to refer to. I found her lectures and explanations to be very helpful. I frequently saw her in office hours, and often times asked questions outside the scope of the class, and she was always able to help me. She is very patient and truly wants each of her students to succeed. No matter the class or student, I have seen her sit down with students very patiently in office hours and explain a concept to them until they get it. Like any math class, they key to success is practice - and she provides an abundance of practice problems in the form of worksheets, quizzes, and old exams. I do think the class could benefit from being just slightly more theory-heavy - thought this is a change she has already expressed interest in making.

Lectures were often broken up into 2 sections with a short break in the middle, and were always recorded with the slides being posted as well. I see a lot of people saying that he's monotone or lectures are boring, however I saw it more so as Pedram wanting to be as straightforward as possible when communicating content. Pedram and the TAs were also very responsive on Piazza for any questions that came up outside of class time. CMSC 131 is just a tough course in general (in my eyes coming from someone who didn't have a lot of programming experience beforehand), however Pedram was always very approachable and helpful if there was something confusing and made it a bit easier. In my opinion, if you're willing to put in the work in classes, you will come away with a good grade, and learn a lot in the process.

Absolutely terrible, if you want a stress free life, don't take her as your professor. taking the summer session currently, and it's making me want to kill myself! lectures are ramble-y, examples are far too busy, and the way we're being taught assembly (ie reading off slides verbatim) is absurd. exams and earlier projects were light but holy shit is this class miserable currently

Fawzi is a solid lecturer, and he does a great job of preparing you for the higher level courses. Even though I'm not a strong math student, I feel like I now have a firm grasp of this material, especially writing proofs. Fawzi made it very clear what you needed to know for the exams, and the grading was pretty relaxed. Overall, this was a great class and I'd recommend Fawzi for any class you can take with him. As long as you put the effort in, you'll get a decent grade and you'll feel confident moving forward.

Max is an INCREDIBLY lazy professor. It truly feels like he puts in 0 time to preparing for lectures because his slides are often incomplete or a mess, he doesn't know the answers to any questions students ask during class (or he gives the vaguest hand-wavy response), and he frequently ends lecture 30 minutes early because he's run out of things to say. It feels like he himself doesn't fully understand what he's teaching sometimes. Like the other reviews note, he also fills a bunch of lecture time with unrelated thoughts and work stories, and while the class seems to find them entertaining (and Max loves the attention and reactions he gets from saying all his unpopular or taboo things), it would be better if there was more real content time to match. Max doesn't believe in studying any of the data science concepts rigorously, and while teaching a survey of topics at a high-level could be acceptable, he doesn't even touch on enough topics to make the class worthwhile. Instead, we learn in an entire semester basically what someone could get from reading a few articles on data science for a few hours. He also assigned multiple hours worth of youtube videos this semester in lieu of teaching the topics himself, and made the content directly testable on the exams. His reading-based exam questions (which constitute a significant portion of each exam grade) are genuinely trivia and not relevant to any fundamental understanding of data science concepts. He isn't active in responding to people's concerns on Piazza, mistakes are abundant in his posted materials, and policies seem to change frequently (such as him announcing a flat 11% curve on exam 1 then never following through on it). Overall I find it difficult to give a higher rating to a professor who transferred such little knowledge to his students and put in such little effort into his full-time teaching job. I excelled in this class (and you definitely can too) by always going to lecture, reviewing the slides carefully before exams, memorizing major points from the readings, and thinking critically about what Max must be looking for while answering exam questions.

Nelson is knowledgeable and teaches the material decently but he is unprofessional. I don't really see the hype. Don't get me wrong, he is good, but so is Fawzi. One of the best professors I have had at UMD. As other reviewers mentioned, she is very responsive on Piazza. She is also very lenient with the deadlines. Goat lecturer but just be aware his grading takes FOREVER. Like at least a month for exams and projects and like a week for final. Everyone here is complaining for no reason, i'm taking this class right now and the exams and projects are challenging but not to the point that some of these reviews are saying. nothing good to say. All the reviews from this year pretty much echo how I feel. I hope Marine Carpuat reads over these reviews and considers modifying the syllabus/course structure for the students taking this next year.
