Genuinely one of the worst structured classes I have ever taken. It felt like they threw the course together without any forethought. The course grades consisted entirely of projects and one midterm which occurred during the first quarter of classes. For a course whose material was centered around projects, the projects themselves felt random, and disorganized, and had a zero-tolerance policy for late submissions. Anything submitted after 11:59 on the due date would result in an instant 0% on the assignment. This has been one of the most stressful experiences of my college career.

For clarity, I'll quickly explain the class format. 5 assignments that are worth 40% of your grade with the lowest score being dropped, one midterm (that is awkwardly placed at about a third of the way through the semester) that is worth 20% of your grade, and a final that is "cumulative" and worth another 40%. There is also a hefty curve in the class which can be upwards of 6-7% some years -- typically depends on the difficulty of the exams that year. Regarding the assignments, they are pretty challenging. They often can take between 10-20 hours (especially dynamic programming one) and lots of work since each problem involves understanding all the underlying concepts, inventing/creating an algorithm, proving it works with some reasonable degree of certainty (instructors tend to be lenient about how "good" your proof is if you're right though), and proving it works in the runtime bound. Definitely start early, and definitely make frequent visits to office hours to bother the TA's and ask them to review through your work since ultimately they are the ones grading the assignments. Regarding the midterm, it was weirdly placed. The midterm was placed at the same time classes that typically have 2 midterms have their fist midterm (around end of first week beginning of second week of October). Otherwise, that midterm was relatively straightforward conent-wise -- those who didn't do well either couldn't brainstorm the gimmick to answer the question on the exam, or simply didn't review and study enough. The average on that exam was about a 68%. The final, in my opinion, was slightly harder. It covers a significantly higher breadth of topics than the midterm. In my opinion, the depth that each question goes into in the topic was a bit lower since most of the questions were very similar to questions on previous practices or other CMSC451 finals practices you could find online. The final on its own isn't that challenging, however, with much of the content being straightforward from the textbook. So long as you practice the standard questions, you really should be fine. The best part of Child's class is lectures. His lectures are just amazing. They are well put-together, easy to follow, and also have just enough "question the class to see what the class is thinking" but enough "let's guide through the class so we get some sh*t done". Laxman (the other well renowned and highly rated CMSC451 teacher who also taught Fall 2024) came and gave in a guest lecture, and I was absolutely surprised in the difference in quality between the lectures. Although Laxman's lecture wasn't "bad", it just really pointed out to me how much Child's lectures have an almost 3blue1brown feel because of how nice they flow. Some other misc things: he's pretty active on Piazza so that's really nice. Some of the TA's don't know a lot about these problems (and that follows because a lot of them naturally don't work in this field and might have other preoccupations), so they might also get stuck or not be able to help out on problems so try and exhaust all the TA's office hours and Child's office hours when stuck on homework. Child's expertise is in quantum algorithms so if you need anything with that or are interested, definitely feel free to talk to him about it. He tries to spend a lecture covering basic quantum algorithms at the end of the course but sometimes he doesn't have time to do that (like this semester), but regardless, you should look into it if interested. Overall, I had a lot of fun in this course and it's a definite recommend (even over other CMSC451 sections -- including Laxman's). While you might not necessarily get much practical implementation value out of the course, it's a lot of fun, and definitely molds your brain to become better and more versed in the world of reading and understanding algorithmic problems (which can be infinitely valuable when doing things like Leetcode or software interviews). If you have any math background or are interested in any algorithms stuff, definitely take the course!

As a CS major, you actively learn some of the applications of Linear Algebra and learn a lot from Professor Wong.

I would give ZERO stars if I would. This is both the hardest and worst course that I've ever had the displeasure of taking at UMD. I enrolled in this class because I thought that Operating Systems is a fundamental and useful skill to learn, even if difficult, but found out that the administration of this class makes this 10x more harder for literally no reason. There are so many things wrong with this course that I wouldn't recommend ANYONE taking it because it's not worth it. First of all, others seemed to like the professor's lecturing ability, but I did not. He goes on tangents all the time and is very unclear in his statements that it is impossible to focus. The slides are comprehensive, but are taken straight from the textbook so that isn't really a credit to the professor. The projects and exams though, that is a different hell. Let's talk projects. Each one is incredibly difficult, and the instructions are HORRIBLE. There is really no valid reason why there should be a spec, slides, and FAQ for EVERY SINGLE PROJECT. The spec is awfully written and flat out wrong about things, the project slides are vague and also have incorrect information. The FAQs don't answer certain questions with any new information, and the fact that an FAQ is even needed for a project means that the instructions are poorly written. And to make things worse, even the spec, slides, and FAQ are sometimes not enough. On a related note, administration for this course was TRULY TERRIBLE. Questions on Piazza were just left unanswered even though there were many people with the same question; the TAs just didn't answer and weren't active. I'm pretty sure they were also left in the dark about logistics in the class, because it was near the end of the semester and we STILL did not have breakdowns of grading. That part of the course website was just never filled out. And one of our pop quizzes, which we only had 10 minutes to do and had a very poor average, was worth almost an entire project grade. That is completely ridiculous and shows how little the professor cares about administration for this class. For exams, we didn't get any review material, no study guide or previous exams, zip, zilch, nada. Just "look at the slides" which are hundreds if not thousands of slides so it's impossible to study everything on it. In addition, for our final, the professor was very unaccommodating to concerns over the Omicron variant, and refused to move the final online despite multiple CS classes shifting online, and almost the entire class requesting this change. No reasoning was given, of course. Lastly, our final exam, which is worth a quarter of our final grade, was put on the grade server, and we never even got it back to see what we got wrong, let alone a regrade request. It was simply put on Testudo. This fact may change since this review is posted, but nevertheless it is inexcusable to have these final grades submitted without students seeing the reason, especially when this resource is easily available via Gradescope. I get that Operating Systems is a hard concept, but like I said, the administration made this course needlessly more difficult. I am sure that most other people in the class agree with me regarding the majority of the points that I raised here, and there are probably more points that I didn't mention. These points are definitely fixable (having clear grading, clear project descriptions, enforcing Piazza answering, giving us study material) and should definitely be addressed the next time this course is taken. I find that unlikely to happen though, so I do not recommend this course to anyone until then. You're better off looking at the slides or textbook on your own.

Flipped classroom model yada yada yada. Judge yourself whether you will actually succeed in that type of environment. Marsh as a professor is knowledgeable and tries to do everything he can for his students. His slides are utterly useless in terms of actually learning what to do, so you will have to do most of the learning on your own (which really doesn't help in the flipped classroom model) or figure it out somehow, which leads me to the the biggest problem with this class: the projects. They are incredibly difficult, no two ways about it. Somehow I managed to complete them but oh boy was it stressful. I also am not really interested in the class content, so that definitely didn't help. Also, one thing to note is that this class HEAVILY leans into computer security rather than network security. Do not think this class's content will give you enough information comparable to 417.

Justin is a great lecturer who really makes the content engaging and easy to digest, and he posts great notes as well if you miss class. The seven exam structure was interesting, but I quite liked it. Given we had a midterm dropped and that the exams generally reflected the given practice material it was not too difficult to prepare for, and I found it less stressful to study one or two topics than studying a bunch of topics for two or three exams. Just start reviewing practice problems and making sure you understand how the exams DS works a couple of days before the exam and you should be good to go. The projects aren't too bad and have no secret test which is nice, and one is dropped. Great class, would recommend.

Mr Regli is a really nice guy and super helpful if you ever talk to him one on one. However, there were countless issues for this course. Projects with conflicting directions, instructions in 5 different places making it hard to know everything, TA "recitations" where they just read off a slide and couldn't answer basic questions, exams where students had to argue for points back due to unclear wording, etc. Easily the most disorganized class I've taken at UMD, making it hard to engage with the material and actually learn. His lectures are also completely all over the place and impossible to follow. By the third week no one was even attempting to take notes because he goes so fast and its not clear which information is relevant at all. For the final, the whole class really struggled because everyone studied the wrong material, myself included. He did curve the exam(s), so in his defense he made up for a lot of his mistakes. I also did get an A in the class, so it all worked out in the end to be fair. However, CMSC421 has been a terrible class at UMD for years.

I genuinely wanted to learn this material, but the way the course was run made that almost impossible. It’s hard to express how much I dislike this course. It’s structured very poorly: it’s extremely fast-paced with almost no room to actually retain the material. The assignments don’t reflect what you need to know to do well on the exams, and the textbooks are pretty unhelpful if you’re new to ML. I’m not even going to say much about the grading (yes, it’s very punitive, likely due mostly to the TAs) because others have already covered that. The instructor seems to assume that if one person gets an A on the midterm, then everyone should be able to get an A, which completely ignores the reality that students juggle many responsibilities. It’s not just “do research,” “teach,” eat, and sleep. Her teaching style ends up overwhelming students and reinforcing unnecessary competition, especially coming from someone who didn’t go through the same level of modern academic pressure, unstable economy, or constant distractions. Overall, the class was mentally draining because of the uncertainty around how to actually learn and retain the material, what to expect on exams, and how to find reliable resources for long-term understanding. By the second midterm, the stress had taken a significant toll on, I’m sure, the majority of the class. Amazing and thank you!

This was the most difficult class I've ever taken at UMD, and I do not know why it was necessary for it to be this way. The participation quizzes in lecture are grading on accuracy, the reading quizzes during the week are difficult, and the exams are absolutely brutal. DVH is alright. Good lectures with plenty of dry humor. Projects are hard outside of the first two but manageable so long as you get started early. Helpful TAs on Piazza (shoutout Pierce). Man. So you thought 433 was always just going to be Java multithreading right? NOPE! Turns out, it's just whatever the professor wants to teach. This guy, Mr. Rance Cleaveland, was all about programming correctly, because in theory, the more correct your code is, the more secure it is. Neat concept. Nice. Cool beans. Quite a shame, because he clearly can't run a class about it. His class is structured around a single paper mathy assignment, several projects in Dafny and Haskell (dafny is extremely cringe and haskell is just ocaml part 2), one midterm, and one final. Oh, you want to study for the midterm or the final? Yeah sure man, all you have to study is a single slide of a presentation showing all the topics you need to know. No example problems. No practice exam. No textbooks. I guess you have the singular homework that wasn't a project. At least the exam is open computer, closed internet, but doesn't really help when you have zilch to study from. For me, his lecture was quite boring and rather un-learn-able for someone who isn't interested in learning what ancient Mesopotamian symbol I need to know this time. The projects were either incredibly easy or extremely annoying and frustrating, either due to the language or the extremely poor project description. There were multiple Piazza questions all asking about what he meant by the projects and he basically answered them full of academic jargon that probably makes sense conceptually. So basically, his class has zero structure and you're supposed to already be a god and know this kinda stuff in order to do well. The class is not easy despite the workload being low. It just felt like he finally found a hundred people or so willing to listen to him talk about whatever he's been studying for the past however many years.

I'd give 4.7 stars if PlanetTerp had such an option. This is a hard class. Not in the way that MATH140/141 are considered "hard", or in the way that Kruskal's classes are "hard" (at least his 351), but rather it is hard by virtue of the material. Algorithms are just often difficult concepts to grasp and really understand to the depth that Childs' wants his students to be able to grasp and understand for his assignments and exams. The class is paced quite nicely for me - I showed up to every lecture, and I feel like I gained something from each one. I was able to ask questions pretty frequently (perhaps too frequently), and Childs' would always spend the time to think about an answer to each one, and I felt that that helped me understand the material greatly. He records all of his lectures and posts all of his notes. The only things from class not available asynchronously online are the Q&A times that he holds in the 5-10 minutes before each class begins. The assignments are hard. (Did I mention the class is hard?) The first two took me about 10 hours each, and the other three 15-20 hours each. Each one is a set of five problems, the answers to which require (unless you're a super-mega-genius I guess) intuition and material from the lectures. A quote from one of his office hours: "If you're stuck on this problem, think about the algorithms we covered in class; I make the homeworks directly related [to those]." - Childs My strategy for the homeworks were to look at the problems when they were assigned, then keep them in mind over the next two weeks of lectures (each assignment is assigned exactly two weeks before they're due). Spending the time to actually understand the material on them is definitely helpful - they're actually harder than the exam questions by a solid margin, and they mirror the exam structure. Also, he drops the lowest of the five assignments, so each of your best four assignments comprise 10% of your final grade. Considering that there is ample time for each one, it's definitely possible to have the assignments be the grade fallback. The exams are hard. (yes.) The midterm is worth 20% of your final grade, and the final 40%. There's definitely a time-crunch aspect to this. As of writing this review, I haven't taken the final yet. But speaking from the midterm experience, there wasn't a single student that left the exam room early (shocker). Although it seemed like most of the class felt pretty bad about the midterm, to Childs', the midterm was "on the easier side." (Avg 69, median 70 iirc) I did well enough not to have major complaints about it, and other reviews go more in-depth. The textbook is... something that I didn't read. I'm sure it was useful to those who did, but the lectures + questions + office hours + assignments prepared me well enough to face the exams. Although Childs' is a great lecturer and all-around smart guy, he's definitely a bit hard to talk to. He feels like a classic computer-focused guy (which is fair, since he's getting paid for it lol), and I definitely agree with the previous reviewer that said it felt impossible to build rapport with him. TL;DR: Great lecturer, fair class, hard af so look at the grade distr. to make your choice

She's a first time professor. In terms of lectures, she did try to make the content more understandable, and I think her explanations do, at times, make a significant improvement to the readings. I am shocked to see so many people up in arms about the high number of midterms in this class. It seems like I am in the minority when I say I didn't mind this structure and actually kind of liked it. Justin changed his CMSC420 course structure this semester to be very largely exam-based, with a "midterm" exam every two weeks. He did this with the idea that if he assigned homework, students would just ChatGPT the whole thing (and he's probably not wrong). At surface level, this does sound atrocious and I was worried at first. But there is a pro to this structure: there were no major midterm exams that required cramming a huge amount of content into your brain, like most classes. Each exam was entirely focused on the material we had covered since the last exam, which was at max two weeks, or five lectures, of material. Thus, there was only so much he could possibly test on, making studying easier (for me at least). The rest of the things that people have praised Justin for over the years haven't gone away: his super engaging lectures, his detailed and organized notes, and his stellar focus on helping students succeed. For every topic we covered, he had a set of organized optional problems on that topic available on ELMS. Before each exam, he would post on Piazza which questions within those problem sets to focus on when studying. So my studying usually consisted entirely of working through those suggested problems, which was enough to get me As on just about every exam. Maybe the material just clicked with me in a way that it didn't for others, but I had to study for like maximum two hours for each exam. As such, I actually liked this structure because for me, it kept the workload outside of class pretty light. Study for an exam one night every two weeks, do the occasional project here and there (these were pretty straightforward, enjoyable, and well-explained). He also drops the lowest exam grade and lowest project grade, so there's a nice cushion for error there too. I'm not sure if he will keep doing this in the future, because he has seen the negative feedback here and elsewhere and has acknowledged that he wasn't aware some students would have such major stress in regards to this class. TL;DR: If you are a student who tends to study a LOT for exams and tends to get really stressed before exams, I would stay away from this class with Justin, because you'll probably fall into the same hole as a lot of these 1-star reviewers. But if you're someone like me who doesn't stress too much over exams, I imagine this class will feel light for you too. Justin is still a top-notch lecturer and professor, and I loved learning this content from him.
